## 10. Explanation of the First Nāga Vimāna

The story shown by the verse beginning with "Susukkakhandhaṃ" is the Nāga Vimāna story. What is the reason for its arising? The Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī. At that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, while wandering on a celestial journey as described below, reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. There, he saw a certain son of the gods riding a great, entirely white celestial elephant, traveling through the sky with a large retinue and great celestial power, illuminating all directions like the moon and the sun. Having seen him, he approached where that son of the gods was. Then, that son of the gods descended from the elephant, respectfully paid homage to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, and stood with palms joined. Then the Elder said:

'Riding an elephant with a very white back, faultless, tusked, powerful, and of great speed,
riding the noble elephant well-adorned, you have come here through the air in the sky.
On the two tusks of the elephant, lotus ponds with clear water and blooming lotuses are created.
In those lotuses, groups of musical instruments are playing, and these enchanting goddesses are dancing.
You have attained celestial success and possess great power. What merit did you perform when you were a human being?
Why do you have such blazing power? Your radiance also shines in all directions.'

Thus, by way of praising his prosperity, he asked about the action he had performed.

In that verse, 'susukkakhandhaṃ' means having a very white back or neck. Although the four legs, the sheath of the penis, the face, both ears, and the tail of that elephant were excluded, the entire body was white; however, because the area of the back and neck was exceptionally whiter, it is called 'susukkakhandhaṃ'. 'Nāgaṃ' means a celestial noble elephant. 'Akācinaṃ' means...
235:
"Faultless" means being free from defects of complexion, such as spots or mottling on the skin. There is also the Pali word "ājānīya," which means possessing the characteristics of a noble thoroughbred. "Dantiṃ" refers to one endowed with broad, grand, and beautiful tusks. "Baliṃ" refers to one who is strong, possessing great power (mahabala). "Mahājavaṃ" refers to one with great speed, who travels swiftly. Furthermore, in the word "abhiruyha," the dropping of the nasal (anunāsika-lopa) should be noted; it means "worthy of being mounted" or "to be ridden." The remaining terms are to be understood in the manner already described.

Thus, the son of the devas, being questioned by the elder, wishing to relate the wholesome deed he had performed in the past, replied with these verses:

"Eight fallen flowers of the Great Sage Kassapa,
I placed upon the stupa, with a confident heart and my own hands.
Because of that deed, I have such a complexion... (etc.) ...
And my radiance shines forth in all directions."

The meaning of these verses is: In the past, at the golden stupa of the Samma-Sambuddha Kassapa, which was one league (yojana) in height, I found eight flowers that had fallen from their stalks at the foot of a bush. Having taken them, with a heart full of faith and a desire to worship, I offered them in homage.

According to the tradition, in the past, after the Samma-Sambuddha Kassapa had attained Parinibbāna and a golden stupa one league in height had been built, King Kikī of Kāsi together with his retinue, the townspeople, the merchants, and the country folk performed flower offerings every day. As they made these daily offerings, flowers became very expensive and difficult to obtain.

Then, a certain lay follower (upāsaka) searched the flower-sellers' street but could not find even a single flower for a kahāpaṇa. Taking eight kahāpaṇas, he went to a flower garden and said to the gardener, "Give me eight flowers for these eight kahāpaṇas." The gardener replied, "Sir, there are no flowers left; they have all been carefully searched for and picked." When the lay follower said, "I will look for them myself," the gardener replied, "If that is the case, enter the garden and search." Entering the garden and searching, the lay follower found eight fallen flowers and said to the gardener, "Friend, take these coins." The gardener said, "You have found them through your own merit; I will not take the coins." The man, thinking, "I do not wish to take flowers without payment to make an offering to the Blessed One," placed the coins before the gardener, took the flowers, and...
236:
...went to the courtyard of the stupa and made the offering with a heart full of faith. Later, after passing away, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Having stayed there for the full lifespan, he wandered from one celestial realm to another repeatedly. Due to the remaining result of that wholesome deed, he was reborn again in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven during the time of our Blessed One's appearance. With reference to this matter, the words "He saw a certain son of the devas in that heaven," and so forth, were stated below.

The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having returned to the human world, reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, taking this incident as the occasion, taught the Dhamma in detail to the assembled audience. That teaching was beneficial to the multitude.

## The Explanation of the Mansion of the Elephant is finished.

## 11. Explanation of the Second Mansion of the Elephant

The story beginning with "Having mounted the great elephant" is the Second Mansion of the Elephant (Dutiya Nāgavimāna). What is the origin of this story? The Blessed One was staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha. At that time, there was a certain lay follower in Rājagaha who was faithful and devoted, established in the five precepts. On Uposatha days, he would observe the Uposatha precepts. In the morning, according to his wealth and means, he would give alms to the Saṅgha of monks. After eating his own meal, he would dress in clean clothes, wrap himself in a clean upper robe, and in the afternoon, usually having the eight kinds of drinks brought along, he would go to the monastery, offer them to the Saṅgha, and approach the Blessed One to listen to the Dhamma. In this way, that lay follower, having respectfully accumulated many good deeds through giving and virtue, passed away from this human life and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. By the power of that deva's merit, a magnificent, entirely white celestial elephant appeared. Mounting that elephant, the son of the devas would occasionally go out to play in the gardens with a large retinue and great celestial power.

Then one day, prompted by a sense of gratitude, he came down from the celestial realm at midnight, riding the celestial elephant with a large retinue, thinking, "I will pay homage to the Blessed One." Illuminating the entire Veḷuvana Monastery, he descended from the elephant's back, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and with hands joined in salutation, stood at a respectful distance...
237:
The deity, having come from the celestial realm and illuminating the entire Veḷuvana Monastery, descended from the back of the elephant, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and stood with palms joined in a certain place. Standing near the Blessed One, the Venerable Vangīsa, with the Blessed One's permission, questioned that deity with these verses:

“Riding a great elephant, a noble tusker entirely white,
You wander from forest to forest, escorted by a host of celestial nymphs.
Illuminating all directions, you are like the star Osadhī.

By what merit do you have such a complexion ...
And your radiance shines in all directions?” (Thus he questioned).

Being thus questioned, that deity also answered the Venerable Vangīsa with these very verses:

“That deity, delighted, being questioned by the Venerable Vangīsa,
Explained the problem, which is the fruit of this action (kamma):

When I was a human being among humans, I was a lay follower of the Visionary One.
I abstained from taking life; I avoided what was not given in the world.

I was not a drinker of intoxicants, nor did I speak lies;
I was content with my own wife.
With a heart of faith, I respectfully gave abundant offerings of food and drink.

Because of that merit, I have such a complexion ...
And my radiance shines in all directions.” (Thus he answered).

In these verses, there is no new or extraordinary word; the remaining meaning is just as described previously.

## The Explanation of the Second Nāgavimāna is finished.
