## 12. Explanation of the Third Nāgavimāna

The Third Nāgavimāna story begins with the verse “Ko nu dibbena yānena.” What is the origin of this Vimāna story? The Blessed One was staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground, near Rājagaha. At that time, three Arahant elders spent the rainy season in a small village. Having completed the rainy season and performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, they set out for Rājagaha, thinking, “We shall pay homage to the Blessed One.” In the evening during their journey, they arrived near a sugarcane field belonging to a Brahmin of wrong view in an unspecified small village and asked the field guard, “Friend... is it possible to reach Rājagaha today?” The field guard replied, “Noble sirs... it is not possible to reach Rājagaha today; Rājagaha is still about two leagues (half a yojana) from here. Please stay here and proceed tomorrow.” When asked, “Is there a suitable monastery for staying in this place?”, he replied, “There is none, venerable sirs, but I will arrange a place for you to stay.” The elders accepted.

That field guard tied wooden sticks in the form of a branch-pavilion right among the growing sugarcane plants, covered it with sugarcane leaves, and spread a layer of straw underneath, then offered it to one elder. For the second elder, he tied three sugarcane stalks in the shape of a tripod, covered it with grass, made a grass bedding underneath, and offered it. For the remaining one, he took out two or three wooden sticks and branches from his own hut, covered them with a robe, made a 'robe-hut,' and offered it. The elders stayed there. Then, when the night had passed and it was dawn, he cooked food early, offered tooth-wood and water for washing the face, and then offered the meal along with sugarcane juice. When those elders had finished their meal, performed the thanksgiving (anumodanā), and were departing, he offered a stalk of sugarcane to each, thinking, “This will be a portion of merit for me.” That donor followed the elders for a short distance on the path and, upon returning, experienced great joy and happiness (pīti-somanassa) on account of the service and the gift he had performed.

The Brahmin owner of the field, coming from the opposite direction of the departing monks, asked the monks, “Venerable sirs, where did you get the sugarcane?” When he heard, “It was given by the field guard,” the Brahmin became angry and displeased. Overcome by rage and making a 'taṭa-taṭa' sound, he chased after the man and, striking him with a club, took his life with a single blow. That field guard, repeatedly recollecting only the meritorious deed he had performed, passed away and was reborn as a deity in the Sudhammā celestial assembly. By the power of his merit, a great, noble, celestial elephant, entirely white, appeared for him.
239:
Upon hearing of the death of the sugarcane field guard, his parents, relatives, and friends went to that place weeping with tears in their eyes; all the villagers also gathered there. In that place, his parents began to perform the funeral rites.

At that moment, that deva son, riding a divine elephant, surrounded by all kinds of musicians, playing five-fold musical instruments, with a large retinue and great divine power, came from the deva world and stood in the sky with a form visible to the assembly. Then, a wise man who was present there asked about the meritorious deeds the deva son had performed in the past with these verses:

“O man, who comes by a divine vehicle, a completely white elephant, who are you? You are being honored in the sky with the sound of musical instruments being played.

Are you a deva, or a gandhabba, or Sakka, the destroyer of cities (Purindada)? Not knowing, we ask you; how may we know you?”

That deva son also explained the matter to him with these verses:

“I am not a deva, nor a gandhabba, nor Sakka, the destroyer of cities. There are devas named Sudhammā; I am one of them.”

“Raising joined palms fully, I ask the deva of the Sudhammā class: having performed what meritorious deed in the human life does one arise in the Sudhammā heaven?” he asked again.

“One who gives a hut made of sugarcane, a hut made of grass, or a hut made of cloth—by giving even one of these three, one arises in the Sudhammā heaven,” the deva son replied again.

In that verse, 'tūriyatāḷitanigghoso' refers to the sound of the five-fold divine musical instruments played in honor of himself. 'Antalikkhe mahīyati' means standing in the sky and being honored by a large retinue while remaining in the sky.
240:
“Devatā nu si” means “Are you a deva? Are you a deity?” “Gandhabbo” means “Are you a deva of the Gandhabba class?” “Adu Sakko Purindado” means “Or are you Sakka, famous as ‘Purindada’ because he used to give gifts in the past, or are you Sakka, the king of devas?” Here, although Sakka and Gandhabba are devas, because they are mentioned separately, according to the logic of ‘the cow and the bull’ (go-balivadda), the word ‘deva’ should be understood as referring to devas other than Sakka and Gandhabba.

Then the deva son, thinking “An answer should correspond to the question,” rejected the status of the deva, gandhabba, or Sakka they asked about, and wishing to make himself known, said “I am not a deva, nor a gandhabba,” and so on. In that context, “I am not a deva” means “I am not just any deva as you suspect, nor a gandhabba, nor Sakka; but indeed, I am one of the devas named Sudhammā.” The Sudhammā class of devas is a specific group within the Tāvatiṃsa assembly. Some say that the sugarcane field guard, having heard of the splendor of those devas, had previously directed his mind toward them.

“Phutuṃ” means having made it great or complete. This is said to show the performance of an act with respect.

The deva son, being asked about the Sudhammā deva vehicle, spoke the verse “Ucchāgāraṃ...” etc., wishing to tell of his own merit by taking only what was seen, like describing the color of a chameleon. In that verse, “giving one of the three” means “Although I gave all three types of huts, this meaning is also fulfilled by giving any one of those three,” and the deva son spoke thus by taking this approach. The rest is easy to understand.

Thus, having answered the meaning they asked, and manifesting the virtues of the Triple Gem, the deva son rejoiced together with his parents and returned to the deva world. The people, hearing the words of the deva son, developed great faith and reverence for the Buddha and the Saṅgha. They prepared many offerings, filled carts, went to Veḷuvana, and gave a great offering (mahādāna) to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, and reported the matter to the Teacher. The Teacher also spoke according to that question and answer, and taking that deva son as the occasion...
241:
(The Blessed One) taught the Dhamma in detail and established them in the refuges and the precepts. Having established faith, they paid homage to the Blessed One, returned to their village, and built a monastery at the place where the sugarcane-field guard (Ucchupāla) had died.

## The Explanation of the Third Nāga Mansion is finished.

## 13. Explanation of the Cūḷaratha Mansion

"Daḷhadhammā nisārassa" and so forth is the Cūḷaratha Mansion story. What is its origin? After the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna and the relics had been distributed and enshrined in stūpas of the Teacher in various places, and after the disciples headed by the Elder Mahākassapa had been selected to conduct the rehearsal of the Dhamma, while they were staying in various places with their respective followers out of compassion for those to be guided (veneyya) until the time for the rains-retreat, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana was staying in a certain forest area in a frontier region. At that time, King Assaka was ruling in the city of Potali in the kingdom of Assaka. The son of that king's chief queen, a prince named Sujāta, when he reached the age of sixteen, was banished from the country by his father due to the persistence of the younger queen. He entered the forest and lived there, relying on hunters.

It is said that this prince had gone forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa and, remaining established in mere virtue, died as a worldling (puthujjana) and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Having stayed there for the full lifespan and wandering only in happy destinations (sugati), thirty years after our Blessed One attained Enlightenment, he was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of King Assaka in the kingdom of Assaka and was born. He was named "Sujāta." He grew up with a large retinue.

When the prince's mother passed away, the king appointed another princess to the position of chief queen. Later, she also gave birth to a son. Seeing the son, the king was pleased and granted her a boon, saying, "Lady, take whatever boon you desire." She kept the boon in mind, and when Prince Sujāta reached the age of sixteen, she said to the king, "Great King, you were pleased upon seeing my son and granted me a boon; please grant that boon now." "Take it,
242:
O Queen," (the king said). "Give the kingship to my son," she requested. "Perish, you low-born woman! While my eldest son Prince Sujāta, who is like a celestial youth, is still here, why do you speak thus?" he rejected. Although the queen pleaded repeatedly, her wish was not fulfilled. One day she said, "Great King, if you stand by the truth, then grant it." The king, feeling remorseful, thought, "I granted this queen a boon without careful consideration, and now she speaks like this." He summoned Prince Sujāta, told him the matter, and shed tears. Seeing his father grieving, the prince became distressed and, shedding tears, said, "Great King, please give me permission; I shall go elsewhere." Hearing this, the king said, "I will build another city for you; live there." But the prince did not desire it. "I will send you to the presence of kings who are my friends," the king said, but the prince did not agree to that either. He simply said, "Great King, I will go to the forest." The king embraced his son, kissed him on the head, and said, "After my passing, return here and establish yourself in the kingship," and then let him go.

While the prince was living in the forest relying on hunters, he went out hunting deer one day. A certain deity, who had been his noble friend when he was a monk (in a previous life), wishing for his welfare, lured him in the form of a deer. After running near the dwelling place of the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, the deer disappeared. The prince, thinking, "I will catch this deer now," ran after it and reached the Elder's dwelling. Not seeing the deer, he saw the Elder sitting outside the leaf-hut and stood near him, leaning on the tip of his bow. The Elder looked at the prince and, knowing his entire history from the beginning, wished to favor him. Acting as if he did not know, he showed hospitality and asked:

"You who stand leaning on a bow of firm nature and excellent heartwood,
Are you a kshatriya of royal lineage, or a hunter wandering in the forest?"

In that verse, "daḷhadhammā" means a firm bow. It is called a bow with the strength of two thousand (men). A bow with the strength of two thousand means that when a weight of iron heads and so forth is tied to the strung bowstring, and the bow is held by the staff and lifted to the length of an arrow, it has the strength to lift that weight off the ground. "Nisārassa" means of supreme heartwood, of distinguished heartwood (referring to the wood).
243:
"Rukkhaassa dhanuṃ" means a bow made of very solid heartwood. "Olubbha" means standing by leaning or supporting oneself. "Rājanyo" means a prince. "Vanecaro" means one who wanders in the forest. Then, that prince, wishing to reveal himself, said: "Venerable sir, I am the son of King Assaka, the ruler of the Assaka kingdom; I am a forest-dweller. People know my name as Sujāta. While entering the great forest in search of deer, I did not see any deer; while standing there without seeing any, I saw you, venerable sir."

In that verse, "Assakādhipatissā" means of King Assaka, the ruler of the Assaka kingdom. By the word "Bhikkhu," he addresses the Elder. "Mige gavesamāno" means searching for deer, wild boar, and so forth; it refers to going out for a hunt. Hearing those words, the Elder, wishing to exchange greetings with the prince, said: "O prince of great merit, welcome to you; your coming is not ill-come. Take water from here and wash your feet. This drinking water is also cool, brought from a mountain cave; O prince, drink from it and sit on the grass mat."

In that verse, "Adurāgataṃ" means being free from an ill-coming. It means: "O prince of great merit, your coming here is a welcome coming; it is not in the least an ill-coming because it generates joy and delight for both you and me." There is also a variant reading "adhunāgataṃ," which means "recently arrived." "Santhatasmiṃ upāvisā" means to sit on the grass mat of that name, rather than sitting on the bare ground. Then the prince, accepting the Elder's words of greeting, said: "Venerable sir, your words are truly beautiful and worth hearing; they are faultless, beneficial, and sweet; you speak having understood the meaning and the cause."
244:
"O noble sage, what is your delight while living in the forest? Please tell me as I ask. Having heard your words, we shall practice the Dhamma that brings welfare." (Thus the prince spoke).

In that verse, 'kalyāṇī' means good or beautiful. 'Savaniyā' means fit to be heard. 'Nelā' means faultless. 'Atthavatī' means associated with or endowed with benefit in this very life and so forth. 'Vaggū' means sweet. 'Mantvā' means having known or having discerned with wisdom. 'Atthaṃ' means not devoid of benefit, or truly bringing benefit.

'Isinisabhā' means a noble sage who is like a thoroughbred among sages. 'Vacanapathaṃ' means speech. Speech itself is called 'vacanapatha' (the path of speech) because it is the means for attaining the meaning. 'Atthadhammapadaṃ samācaremase' means we shall practice the group of teachings such as virtue (sīla) which bring benefit in this life and the next.

Now the Elder, wishing to speak of his own good practice which was suitable for the prince, said:

"O prince, non-violence towards all beings is pleasing to us. Abstaining from theft, from sexual misconduct, and from drinking intoxicants (is pleasing to us).

Abstinence, balanced living, great learning, and gratitude—these qualities are praiseworthy even in this very life; these are qualities to be praised."

In that verse, 'ārati samacariyā ca' means far-removed abstinence from the aforementioned unwholesome states and the practice of balanced wholesome states such as bodily composure. 'Bāhusaccaṃ' means having great learning in the scriptures (pariyatti). 'Kataññutā' means knowing the help others have done for oneself. 'Pāsaṃsā' means to be praised in various ways by clansmen who desire benefit. 'Dhammā ete' means the qualities like non-violence mentioned above. 'Pasaṃsiyā' means to be praised by the wise.

In this way, the Elder spoke of the good practice suitable for the prince. Then, looking at the prince's life-span with the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa), he saw that the prince had only five months to live. To cause him a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and to establish him firmly in that good practice, he spoke this verse:
245:
## 
“Prince, your death is near; it will be within five months. Prince, know this fact and free yourself from the suffering of the lower realms.”

In that verse, ‘attānaṃ parimocaya’ means to liberate yourself from the suffering of the lower realms.

Then, the prince, wishing to ask for the means of his liberation, said:
“Venerable Sir, to which country should I go, what work should I do, what manly task should I perform, or by what science could I become ageless and immortal?”

In that verse, ‘katamaṃ svāhaṃ’ should be resolved as ‘katamaṃ su ahaṃ’, meaning ‘in what way?’. In the phrase ‘kiṃ kammaṃ kiñca porisaṃ’, the elided verb ‘katvā’ (having done) should be understood. ‘Porisaṃ’ refers to the duty or task of men.

Then, the Elder spoke these verses to preach the Dhamma to the prince:
“Prince, there is no such place where a being, having gone there, could become ageless and immortal. There is no such work, science, or manly effort that can achieve this.

There are kings who possess great wealth, great enjoyments, who rule over kingdoms, and have abundant riches and grain; yet even they are not ageless and immortal.

If you have heard of the sons of Andhakaveṇḍu, who were powerful, heroic, and capable of crushing their enemies; even they reached the end of their lives and perished, unlike the eternal sun and moon.

Khattiyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vessas, Suddas, Caṇḍālas, and Pukkusas—these and others of various births are also not ageless and immortal.

Those who recite the Vedas, which consist of the six limbs and were conceived by the Great Sages, and others with various sciences—they too are not ageless and immortal.

Even the noble sages (isayo) who are peaceful, self-controlled, and devoted to asceticism, eventually abandon their bodies when the time comes.

Even the Arahants, who have developed their minds, finished their tasks, and are free from taints (anāsava), lay down this body when their merit and demerit are exhausted.”

In that verse, ‘yatttha gantvā’ means a place where one might become ageless and immortal by going there and applying effort through work, science, manly duty, physical exertion, or other means. ‘Mahadhanā’ refers to those who possess wealth stored up to the amount of a hundred crores and so on. ‘Mahābhogā’ refers to those who have great daily expenditures, such as three pots of coins and so on. ‘Raṭṭhavanto’ refers to kings who rule over kingdoms spanning many leagues (yojana). ‘Khattiya’ refers to those of the warrior-noble caste. ‘Pahūtadhanadhaññā’ means...
246:
In that verse, "yatttha gantvā" means a place where one might become ageless and immortal by going there and reaching it through work, science, manly effort, or through physical or other types of exertion.

Those who possess great wealth, having collected and stored it to the extent of at least a hundred crores, are called "mahadhana" (the wealthy). Those who have great enjoyments, such as daily expenditures of about three pots of coins, are called "mahābhoga" (those of great enjoyments). "Raṭṭhavanto" refers to the lords of the land, those who govern and rule over kingdoms many leagues in extent. "Khattiya" refers to those of the warrior-noble caste. "Pahūtadhanadhaññā" refers to those who have accumulated much wealth and grain, enough to sustain their retinue for seven or eight years. Even they are not ageless and immortal, but are subject to old age and death. Having such great wealth and so on cannot prevent old age and death from falling upon them.

"Andhakaveṇḍu-puttā" refers to those famously known as the sons of Andhakaveṇḍu. "Surā" means those endowed with power. "Vīrā" means those endowed with energy and effort. "Vikkantappahārino" means those who, by their bravery and heroism, are accustomed to striking and overwhelming the strength of their enemies. "Viddhasthā" means they have perished. "Sassatīsamā" means that although they were like the sun, moon, and stars which endure through generations, those famous individuals also had lineages that lasted only for a short time.

"Jātiyā" means by one's own birth or caste. It implies that even a very noble birth cannot prevent old age and death for them.

"Manta" refers to the Vedas. "Chaḷaṅga" refers to being endowed with the six limbs known as Kappa (Ritual), Byākaraṇa (Grammar), Nirutti (Exegesis), Sikkhā (Phonetics), Chandoviciti (Prosody), and Jotisa (Astronomy). "Brahmacintitaṃ" means that which was conceived by noble sages such as Aṭṭhaka and others, or seen with the eye of wisdom.

"Santā" refers to those with peaceful bodily and verbal actions. "Saññatattā" refers to those with restrained minds. "Tapassino" refers to those who practice austerities that burn away defilements.

Now, the prince, wishing to state his own duty, said:
"O Great Sage, the verses you have spoken are well-said and full of meaning. I have been made to see and understand through this sublime meaning; please be my refuge."
247:
The prince replied: In that statement, 'nijjhattomhi' means "I have reached a state of thorough understanding or satisfaction through the perception known as the essence of the Dhamma." 'Subhatthena' means "by the well-spoken words."

Then the Elder, wishing to instruct the prince, spoke this verse:
'Do not go to me for refuge; go to Him for refuge, the Great Hero of the Sakyan clan, whom I have gone to for refuge.'

Then the prince (Rājakumāra) said:
'Venerable Sir, in which country does your Teacher, the Buddha, reside? I too shall go to see that Victorious One (Jina), the peerless person.'

Again, the Elder said:
'In the eastern country, there was a Great Man born of the Okkāka clan; He has, however, attained Parinibbāna.'

In that verse, "in the eastern country" was said because the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa) is to the east of the place where the Elder was staying.

Thus, the prince, having heard the Elder's Dhamma teaching and having a confident mind, became established in the three refuges and the precepts. Referring to that, it is said:
'Venerable Sir, if your Teacher, the Buddha, were still alive, I would travel a thousand leagues to attend upon Him.

Venerable Sir, although your Teacher has attained Parinibbāna, I go for refuge to that Great Hero even though He has attained Nibbāna.

I go for refuge to the Buddha, and to the unsurpassed Dhamma, and I go for refuge to the Saṅgha of the Teacher of gods and men.

I quickly refrain from taking life; I avoid what is not given in the world; I shall not be a drinker of intoxicants; I do not speak falsehood; and I shall be content with my own wife.'
248:
Thus, to the prince who was established in the refuges and precepts—having said, "I go for refuge to the Buddha who has attained Parinibbāna... I shall be content with my own wife"—the Elder said: "Prince, there is no benefit in your staying here in the forest. Your life will not last long; you will pass away within five months. Therefore, return to your father and perform meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna), so that you may be destined for heaven." Having said this, he gave him the relics he had and sent him away.

As he was leaving, the prince said, "Venerable Sir, I shall go from here according to your words. Please come there out of compassion for me." Knowing the Elder's acceptance, he paid homage, circumambulated him, went to his father's city, entered the garden, and had his arrival reported to the King.

Hearing this, the King went to the garden with his retinue, embraced the prince, took him to the palace, and wished to consecrate him as king. The prince said, "Your Majesty, my life is very short; I will die after four months from today. What use is kingship to me? I will only perform meritorious deeds depending on you." He then made known the virtues of the Elder and the power of the Triple Gem. Hearing this, the King was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and, with a mind confident in the Triple Gem and the Elder, had a great monastery (vihāra) built and sent a messenger to the Venerable Mahākaccāyana. The Elder, wishing to favor the King and the people, arrived. The King and his retinue went out to meet him from afar, escorted the Elder to the monastery, and, respectfully serving him with the four requisites, became established in the refuges and precepts.

The prince also undertook the precepts, respectfully served the Elder and the monks, gave gifts (dāna), and listened to the Dhamma. After four months, he passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Due to the power of his merit, a chariot adorned with the seven kinds of jewels, seven leagues in size, appeared, and many thousands of celestial nymphs became his retinue.

The King performed the funeral rites for the prince's body, offered a great gift (mahādāna) to the Saṅgha of monks, and made offerings to the cetiya. A great crowd of people gathered there, and the Elder also arrived at that place with his retinue. Then the deity (the former prince), looking at the wholesome deeds he had performed and being grateful, thought, "I will go and pay homage to the Elder and make the virtues of the Dispensation (Sāsana) manifest." He mounted his divine chariot and, appearing with a great retinue and a radiant form, arrived, descended from the chariot, and at the Elder's feet...
249:
(The deva), having paid respects to his father (King Assaka) and exchanged pleasantries, approached the Elder and stood with his palms joined in salutation. The Elder questioned that deva with these verses:

“O renowned deva, just as the sun with its thousand rays, possessing great radiance, illuminates the quarters as it traverses the sky in due order, so too is this great chariot of yours. It measures seven yojanas all around.

It is covered all over with plates of gold, and its front is exquisitely adorned with pearls and gems. Well-fashioned engravings of gold and silver, made of beryl, make it beautiful.

This front of the chariot is fashioned from beryl, and this yoke is intricately crafted with rubies. These horses, swift as the speed of mind and adorned with gold and silver trappings, are truly beautiful.

You stand upon this golden chariot like Sakka, the lord of devas, who has a thousand-horse carriage. I ask you, O glorious and wise deva, how did you obtain such magnificent splendor?”

In those verses, ‘Sahasaraṃsī’ refers to the sun. The sun is called ‘Sahasaraṃsī’ because it possesses many thousands of rays. ‘Yathāmahapphabho’ means having a radiance appropriate to its greatness. Just as there is no circle of light equal to the great orb of the sun, the same is true of its radiance. Indeed, in a single moment, that sun stands diffusing light over the three great continents. ‘Dissaṃ yathā bhāti nabhe anukkamaṃ’ means in whatever manner it illuminates and shines upon the quarters as it moves in due order through the sky. ‘Tathāpakkāro’ means having such an appearance. ‘Tavāyaṃ’ is the compound ‘tava ayaṃ’ (this of yours).”
250:
‘Suvaṇṇapaṭṭehi’ means with plates made of gold. ‘Samantamotthaṭo’ means covered all around. ‘Urassa’ refers to the chest of that chariot; the chest of the chariot refers to the base of the chariot pole (the axle-base). ‘Lekhā’ refers to the engravings such as floral and creeper designs made of beryl. Because those engravings are clearly visible on the gold and silver plates, it is said, ‘suvaṇṇassa ca rūpiyassa ca’. ‘Sobhenti’ means they beautify the chariot.

‘Sīsaṃ’ refers to the front of the chariot pole. ‘Veḷuriyassa nimmitaṃ’ means created with beryl, meaning made of beryl gems. ‘Lohitakāya’ means with the ruby called lohitaka, or with any red-colored gem. ‘Yuttā’ means yoked. Alternatively, ‘yuttā suvaṇṇassa ca rūpiyassa ca’ refers to the cords or chains fashioned from gold and silver ornaments.

‘Adhiṭṭhito’ means standing there, having overwhelmed this entire place with his own divine power. ‘Sahasavāhana’ means like Sakka, the lord of devas, whose chariot is yoked with a thousand noble horses. ‘Yasavantā’ is a form of address, meaning ‘O glorious one’. ‘Kovidaṃ’ means one who possesses skillful wisdom, or one who is skilled in chariot riding. ‘Ayaṃ uḷāro’ means ‘In what way did you, O deva, obtain such noble and great splendor?’

Being thus questioned by the Elder, the deva replied with these verses:

“Venerable Sir, in my previous life, I was a prince named Sujāta.
You, out of compassion, established me in the practice of self-restraint and virtue.

Knowing that my life span was coming to an end, you gave me a relic of the Teacher, saying, ‘Prince Sujāta, worship this relic of the Buddha; it will be for your benefit.’

I worshipped that relic with perfumes and garlands with great diligence, and upon discarding my human body, I was reborn in the Nandana Grove.

In the delightful Nandana Grove, filled with various flocks of birds, I rejoice, surrounded by celestial nymphs, with dance and song.”

In those verses, ‘sarīraṃ’ refers to the bodily relic. ‘Hehiti’ means it will come to be. ‘Samuyyuto’ means being very diligent without negligence. Thus, after the deva had answered the Elder’s questions, he paid homage to the Elder, performed a clockwise circumambulation, took leave of his father King Assaka, and returned to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven by chariot. The Elder then related that matter back to the King.
251: 1012-3. In those verses, 'sarīraṃ' refers to the bodily relics. 'Hehiti' means it will be. 'Samuyyutto' means one who is well-exerted or intensely striving. Thus, the deva son, having answered the matter asked by the Elder, paid homage to the Elder, performed a circumambulation, took leave of his father (King Assaka), and mounting his chariot, returned to the celestial world. The Elder also, taking that matter as the occasion, preached the Dhamma in detail to the assembled crowd. That Dhamma talk was beneficial to the multitude. Then the Elder reported all that matter, exactly as it had been spoken by himself and the deva son, to the Dhamma-reciters at the time of the Council; and they included it in the collection accordingly. ## The Commentary on the Cūḷaratha Mansion is finished. ## 14. Commentary on the Mahāratha Mansion The Vimāna story beginning with "Sahassayuttaṃ hayavāhanaṃ subhaṃ" is the Mahārathavimāna story. What is its origin? The Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana monastery in Sāvatthī. At that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, while wandering on a celestial tour according to the method mentioned above, appeared near a deva son named Gopāla in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Gopāla was coming out of his mansion, mounting a great divine chariot yoked with a thousand horses, and heading to the garden for play with a large retinue and great divine power. Seeing the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, the deva son, with deep respect and reverence, quickly descended from the chariot, approached him, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, and stood with his hands raised in salutation over his head. This was his previous deed: It is said that he had worshipped the Blessed One Vipassī with a golden garland and made a wish: "By the power of this merit, may I have a golden breast-ornament garland in every birth." After wandering only in happy destinies for many aeons, during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he was born as a Brahmin teacher named Gopāla to a princess who was like a celestial maiden. She was the daughter of King Kikī of Kāsi, born from the womb of the chief queen, and was named "Uracchadamālā" because she obtained a golden garland according to her previous wish. That Brahmin Gopāla provided great gifts such as the Peerless Alms (Asadisadāna) to the Blessed One Kassapa and the community of disciples. However, because his faculties were not yet mature, for himself and the princess, the Teacher...
252:
...although he listened to the Dhamma, he was unable to attain the special distinction of the Paths and Fruits. Having died as a worldling (puthujjana), by the power of the merit he had accumulated, he was reborn in a golden mansion a hundred leagues in size in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. That deva had a retinue of many crores of celestial nymphs. A divine thoroughbred chariot appeared for him, made of the seven kinds of jewels, yoked to a thousand horses, adorned with well-proportioned walls, having a smooth and sweet sound, and appearing to mock the orb of the sun with the mass of its own radiance.

Having enjoyed celestial bliss there for the full lifespan, and wandering repeatedly only in the celestial realms, in this Buddha-arising era, by the remainder of the result of that same karma, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as the deva named Gopāla, endowed with the wealth and prosperity mentioned above. Referring to that, it was said: 'At that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna... (etc.) ...stood with his hands joined in reverence above his head.' Then, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna questioned the deva who stood there having approached him, with these verses:

'Mounted on this beautiful, manifoldly ornate chariot, yoked to a thousand horses, with horses as your vehicle, you travel around the park, looking as beautiful as Vāsava, the lord of beings, the giver in the past (Purindada). Both your chariot poles are made of gold, perfectly joined at the ends and the shoulders. The well-constructed hubs, finished by heroes among men (skilled craftsmen), shine like the full moon on the fifteenth day. This chariot, covered with golden nets and adorned with many various jewels, has a very pleasant and beautiful sound, and shines with the devas holding yak-tail whisks in their hands.'
253:
These naves of the wheels seem as if created by the mind, and are decorated in the middle of the wheels which are the base of the chariot. These naves are ornate with countless streaks; having countless parts, they shine brilliantly like a flash of lightning.

This chariot is covered with various ornate objects, and the large rims have a thousand rays. The pleasant sound of those chariots is heard like the playing of a five-piece musical ensemble.

On the top, the ornate ring like a moon-disk made of rubies is always pure, pleasing, and radiantly bright. It is perfectly joined with golden streaks and is as beautiful as streaks of beryl.

These horses also have rings in the shape of a moon-disk made of rubies; they are full of strength, have a graceful gait, and are comparable to Great Brahmā. They have large bodies, great power, physical strength, and great speed; knowing your mind, they act exactly according to your wish.

These horses, moving in unison with their four legs, know your mind and act exactly according to your wish. These best of horses are gentle in nature, do not cause terror to the rider, and being joyful, they carry you in harmony.

They shake their manes, they leap, and they fly into the sky. They especially shake their well-made horse-ornaments; the pleasant sound of those horse-ornaments is heard like the sound of a five-piece drum ensemble.

The sound of the chariot, the sound of the ornaments, the sound of the hooves, and the sound produced without distressing the horses—this combined, extremely pleasant sound is heard like the music of the Gandhabba devas in the ornate Cittalatā Grove.
254:
Those goddesses, with eyes as soft as a deer's, with curved eyelashes, smiling faces, and sweet speech, covered in nets of lapis lazuli, with soft and smooth skin, and always worshipped by the Gandhabba deities, are stationed upon the chariot.

Wearing garments of crimson and gold, with large and wide eyes, especially dark eyes, born of noble lineage, with beautiful bodies and graceful smiles, those goddesses stand attending with hands joined in reverence upon the chariot.

Wearing bracelets and ornaments of pure gold, with fine garments, beautiful waists, thighs smooth like banana trunks, and firm breasts, with rounded fingers and lovely, attractive faces, those goddesses stand attending with hands joined in reverence upon the chariot.

Other goddesses, with beautiful braids and exceedingly graceful hair, radiant with uniform beauty, their hair intertwined, following your will and delighting your heart, also stand attending with hands joined in reverence upon the chariot.

Wearing garlands, their bodies covered with white and red lotuses, adorned and anointed with the essence of sandalwood, following your will and delighting your heart, those goddesses stand attending with hands joined in reverence upon the chariot.

Wearing garlands, their bodies covered with white and red lotuses, adorned and anointed with the essence of sandalwood, following your will and delighting your heart, those goddesses stand attending with hands joined in reverence upon the chariot.

The ornaments worn on your neck, hands, feet, and head illuminate the ten directions in every way, like the sun shining in the autumn season.
255:
The flower garlands and ornaments on the arms, swaying by the force of the wind, produce a pleasant, pure, and beautiful sound, worthy of being heard by all the wise.

O deity, the sounds of the chariots, elephants, and musical instruments stationed on both sides of the garden ground delight that deity, just as the sound of the lute played by those with arms like lotus petals delights the multitude.

When the heart-stirring and joyful sounds arise from these many melodious lutes of delightful form, the celestial maidens, well-trained in their arts, wander about dancing upon the lotuses.

Whenever the singing, the music, and the dancing harmonize as one, then some celestial maidens dance there. Some noble women also illuminate the quarters with their radiance.

You, O deity, awakened by the joy of the musical ensemble, dwell in delight like Sakka, the wielder of the thunderbolt (Vajirāvudha), who is worshipped by the gods. These many melodious lutes of delightful form produce heart-stirring and joyful sounds.

O deity, what kind of meritorious deed did you perform yourself in your past life when you were a human? What kind of Uposatha did you observe? What kind of Dhamma practice or vow did you take delight in?

This extensive power and majesty of yours is not the result of a small deed or an Uposatha poorly observed in the past. You delight greatly among the host of devas. (Is this the fruit of your generosity, virtue, or act of salutation? Please answer my question.)
256:
“Is this the fruit of your generosity (dāna), or perhaps of your virtue (sīla), or of your act of salutation (añjali)? Being asked, please tell me that.”

In that verse, 'Sahassayuttaṃ' means yoked with a thousand, or a chariot to which a thousand horses are well-attached. To what does this 'thousand' refer? Since 'Hayavāhanaṃ' is mentioned immediately after, it is understood as a thousand horses. Because horses are his vehicle, it is called 'Hayavāhana'. Some teachers explain 'Sahassayutta-hayavāhanaṃ' as a single compound word by dropping the nasal (anunāsika); in this view, 'Hayavāhana' has the same meaning as 'Vāhana' (vehicle). It means a vehicle yoked with a thousand horses. Other teachers say 'Sahassayuttaṃ' means yoked with a thousand divine thoroughbred horses. 'Sandanaṃ' refers to the chariot. 'Nekacittaṃ' means having various and diverse wonderful decorations. 'Abhito uyyānabhūmiṃ' means near the garden ground. The accusative case is used here in the sense of the possessive (genitive) in relation to the word 'abhito'. Some read it as 'Uyyānabhūmyā', but they do so without considering the grammatical rules. The connection should be seen as: "When proceeding in order, you shine like Vāsava (Sakka), the giver to the gods and the lord of beings."

'Sovaṇṇamayā' means made of gold. 'Te' means your. 'Rathakubbara ubho' refers to the two railings (vedikā) on both sides of the chariot's shoulders. For the beauty of the chariot and for the safety of those standing above, railings are provided on both sides. In the front part of that enclosure, on both sides up to the chariot pole (rathīsā), there is a specific part of the chariot suitable for holding with the hands; here, that very part is intended as 'kubbara'. That is why it says 'ubho' (both). In other places, however, the chariot pole itself is called 'kubbara'. 'Phalehi' refers to the two ends, right and left, which support the chariot. Here, the extremities are called 'phala'. 'Aṃsehi' refers to the lower parts (shoulders) situated at the ends of the kubbara. 'Atīva saṅgatā' means very well-joined, closely fitted, without any gaps. This description applies the characteristics of a man-made chariot crafted with skill to that celestial chariot. However, that celestial chariot is not man-made; it is self-arisen due to one's own karma, not constructed by anyone. 'Sujātagumbā' means having handrails that are a collection of well-formed pillars. Because of the strength of the clusters of pillars that stand without gaps in the railing and have well-formed parts like jars, they are called 'sujāta' (well-formed).
257:
Due to the combination of those lathe-turned pillars, it is called "Sujātagumba." "Naravīraniṭṭhitā" means they are like those completed by master craftsmen. Master craftsmen are called "heroic among men" (naravīra) here because they skillfully execute their craft through the power of energy, without considering their own physical exhaustion. Alternatively, "Naravīra" is a vocative address to the deva. "Niṭṭhitā" means reaching completion and surpassing in perfect beauty. Or there is a reading "Naravīranimmitā," meaning it is as if created by those among men who are endowed with steadfastness. Because of such lathe-turned pillars, this chariot of yours is beautiful. How beautiful? It is as beautiful as the full moon on the fifteenth day of the waxing fortnight.

"Suvaṇṇajālāvatato" means covered with small golden nets. There is also a reading "Suvaṇṇajālāvitato," meaning covered with radiance. "Bahūhi" means with many. "Nānāratanehi" means with various gems such as rubies (padumarāga) and topaz (phussarāga). "Sunandighoso" means having a sound that is well-pleasing, a sweet sound that is pleasant to hear. Or "Sunandighoso" means having a well-made joyful sound, a sound of delight made by shouts of "Sādhu" and so on that arise when watching dances and such. Some also say it is a joyful sound well-employed by way of blessings from time to time. "Subhassaro" means having the nature of shining very brightly, or having a good sound due to the beautiful singing and instrumental music of the devas present in that mansion. "Cāmarahatthabāhubhi" means with arms holding yak-tail whisks, with the arms of devas holding clusters of yak-tail whisks being waved here and there. Or it is beautiful with devas of such a nature.

"Nābhyo" refers to the hubs of the chariot wheels. "Manasābhinimmitā" means they are as if created by the mind, thinking, "Let these hubs be like this." "Rathassa pādantaramajjhabhūsitā" means decorated by the rims (nemi) which are the ends of the wheels (the feet of the chariot), and by the middle of the spokes (ara) which are radiant with various gems. "Satarājicittitā" means variegated with many colors and hundreds of lines or streaks. "Sateratā vijjuriva" means they shine brilliantly like a streak of lightning called "saterata."
258:
"Anekacittāvatato" means well-interspersed (pervaded) with various wonderful works such as floral patterns and paintings. They also recite "Anekacittāvitato"; the meaning is the same, but the sound is lengthened (dīgha) for the sake of ease in the verse. "Puthū ca nemī ca" means having broad and large rims (nemi). The single word "ca" is merely a particle (nipāta). "Sahassaraṃsiko" means having more than a thousand rays. There is also a Pali version "Sahassaraṃsiyo." Other teachers recite "Natā raṃsiyo." There, "natā" refers to the rim sections that are curved like a bow. "Sahassaraṃsiyo" refers to the nets of rays flashing like the orb of the sun. "Tesaṃ" refers to the rim sections that have hanging nets of tinkling bells.

"Sirasmiṃ" means on the head, meaning at the head (top) of the chariot. Or it means at the top of this chariot. "Cittaṃ" means wonderful. "Maṇicandakappitံ" means an ornament inlaid with circles made of gems, an ornament inlaid with moon-like gems. By the phrase "ruciraṃ pabhassaraṃ," the similarity of that gem-ornament to the moon's orb is made clear. By the phrase "sadā visuddhaṃ," it shows that this ornament is even more exceptionally pure than the moon's orb. "Suvaṇṇရာဇီဟိ" means with golden streaks existing in circular forms at intervals. "Saṅgataṃ" means well-joined, smooth, and elegant. "Veḷuriyarājīvā" means it is beautiful like lapis lazuli streaks because of the gem-circles inlaid with golden streaks at intervals. They also recite "Veḷuriyarājīhi."

"Vāဠီ" refers to horses with full tails. There is also a reading "Vājī." "Maṇicandakappitā" refers to horse trappings inlaid with moon-like gems at the places where yak-tail whisks are suspended. "Ārohakambū" means having height and a girth proportionate to that height, being endowed with both height and circumference. "Sujavā" means having beautiful speed, being endowed with speed, having great speed, or having a beautiful gait. "Brahūpamā" means comparable to Brahma, appearing larger than their natural size. "Brahā" refers to horses that are large and endowed with all well-developed major and minor limbs. "Mahantā" refers to horses with great majesty and great psychic power. "Balino" refers to horses endowed with strength, both physical strength and the strength of effort. "Mahājavā" means having swift speed. "Mano tava ñāya" means having known your mind. "Tatheva" means exactly in accordance with the mind. "Siṃsare" means they proceed well.

The word "ime" refers to the aforementioned horses. "Sabbe" means all the horses, numbering about a thousand. "Sahitā" means being united in their movement because of equal speed and equal gait, having a movement that is neither more nor less than each other. With four feet...
259:
They are called 'Catukkama' because they walk with four legs. The meaning already expressed by the word 'Sahita' is made clearer by the phrase 'they carry evenly.' These horses are gentle in nature and are noble thoroughbreds. Therefore, the word 'Anuddhata' is used, meaning they are steady and do not cause agitation. Being non-violent, they carry [the chariot] joyfully, making their mutual delight known to each other and to the chariot riders.

They shake their manes, neck-hairs, and tails. Sometimes they travel with a gait where their hoofprints overlap. Sometimes they move by leaping. Some read 'Plavanti,' but the meaning is the same. They vigorously shake the horse ornaments, such as small bells, which were well-crafted and created by skilled artisans. The sounds of those horse ornaments also emerge.

The aforementioned sound of the chariot and the sound of the ornaments are also heard. 'Apiḷandhana' is also a synonym for ornament. The sound of the horses' hooves striking is also heard. Although these horses travel through the sky, it is said that due to the kamma that produces the pleasant sound of hoofbeats, a striking sound is obtained at every step. Sounds arise because of the great exertion of the horses and because of the neighing of the horses from time to time. The sound of the assembled deities is also heard very melodiously and sweetly. It is just like the sound of the five-fold musical ensemble of the Gandhabba deities in the Cittalata Grove. The sound produced depending on the instruments is itself called 'instruments' (tūriya). In some versions, it is 'vicitrapavane.'

Those goddesses standing on the chariot have soft and smooth eyes like young deer. They have thick eyelashes like those of a calf. They have smiling faces. They speak pleasant words. They are covered with nets of lapis lazuli (veḷuriya). They always receive the offerings of the Gandhabba deities and other noble deities. They have delightful complexions.
260:
The meaning is: 'Piyaṃvadā' refers to those who speak pleasant words. 'Veḷuriyajālavatata' refers to those whose bodies are covered with nets made of lapis lazuli gems. 'Tanucchavā' refers to those with delicate complexions. 'Sadevā' means always, at all times. 'Gandhabbasūraggapūjitā' refers to those honored by Gandhabba deities and other superior deities.

Those goddesses, having delightful complexions, wear red and yellow garments. 'Abhirattalocanā' refers to those whose eyes are beautified by particularly red streaks. 'Kule sujātā' refers to those well-born in the Sindh horse lineage (or) born in the noble host of deities. 'Sutanū' refers to those with beautiful bodies. 'Sucimhitā' refers to those with pure smiles.

Those goddesses wear armlets made of gold. 'Sumajjhimā' refers to those with slender waists. 'Ūruthanūpapannā' refers to those endowed with perfect thighs and breasts; thighs like plantain trunks and breasts like [rounded] caskets. 'Vaṭṭaṅguliyo' refers to those with fingers that are rounded in sequence. 'Sumukhā' refers to those with beautiful or joyful faces. 'Sudassanā' refers to those who are lovely to behold.

'Aññā' refers to some other goddesses. 'Suveṇī' refers to those with beautiful braided hair. 'Susū' refers to those who are young. 'Missakesiyo' refers to those with hair coils mixed with red flowers and such. How so? The connection is: they have hair mixed with hair coils that are similar to each other, arranged in various ways, decorated with gold threads and pearls, and radiant like sapphires, emeralds, and so on. 'Anubbatā' refers to those whose actions are appropriate. 'Tā' refers to those goddesses (accharā).

'Candanasāravositā' refers to those anointed and covered with the essence of divine sandalwood.

'Kaṇṭhesu' and the following words show the ornaments worn on the neck, hands, feet, and head. 'Obhāsayantī' is connected as: they shine with the ornaments on their necks. The same method applies to the remaining words. 'Abbhuddayaṃ' means rising; there is also a reading 'Abbhuddasaṃ,' and the meaning is the same. 'Sāradiko' means occurring in the autumn season (Sarada). 'Bhāṇumā' refers to the sun. That sun, being free from impurities such as clouds, illuminates the ten directions well.

'Vātassa vegena ca' means it occurs by the force of the wind blowing as if offering pleasant scents and sounds, and by the speed of the chariot and horses.
261:
“Muñcantī” means they release (the sound). “Ruciraṃ” means a sound that gives successive delight, like the five-fold musical instruments. “Suciṃ” means a pure sound, unmixed with other things. “Subhaṃ” means a pleasant sound. “Sabbehi viññūhi sutabbarūpaṃ” is construed as: they release a sound that is worthy of being heard by all wise ones skilled in the Gandhabba arts, pleasant to the ear, and of a noble nature.

“Uyyānabhūmyā” means in the garden ground. “Duvaddhato” means from the two sides. Some also read “Dubhato ca ṭhitā”; the meaning is the same. “Rathā” means in the chariot; “nāgā” means in the elephant. Here, the nominative case (paccattavacana) is used in the sense of the accusative (or locative). “Saro” means the sound arising in dependence on the chariot, elephant, and musical instruments. “Devinda” is an address (ālapana) to the deva. “Vīṇā yathā pokkharapattabāhubhi” means: just as a lute (vīṇā), when played according to various scales (mucchanā) with its resonator, neck, and strings well-joined, delights the listeners, so do those chariots and so forth delight with their own sound. Alternatively, it means: just as a lute played by the hands of a lute-player who has reached excellence through being well-trained delights the multitude, so do those chariots and so forth delight with their own sound.

In the verse “Imāsu vīṇāsu,” the summary meaning is: among these many lutes with various types such as Ujukoṭi, Vaṅka, Brahatī, Nandinī, and Tisara, which are beautiful because of their smooth and sweet sound, and thus pleasant in appearance—when the cause of joy (pīti) that stirs the heart, reaches the heart, and captures the heart is played, the celestial nymphs (accharā), due to the impulse of joy and their own well-trained skill, wander about showing their dance among the divine lotuses.

The word “Imāni” should be applied respectively as: “these songs, these instrumental musics, and these dances.” “Samenti ekato” means they have a unified taste (rasa), or they make them have a unified taste. It means that by comparing the sound of the strings with the sound of the song, and the sound of the song with the sound of the strings, they harmonize the tastes such as laughter obtained through dancing, without letting them diminish. “Athettha naccanti” means: furthermore, they dance here. “Athettha accharā obhāsayanti” means: furthermore, other nymphs illuminate. Thus, while making the songs and so forth have a unified taste, some nymphs dance in this chariot of yours. Other noble women, while watching the dance, with the radiance of their own bodies and the radiance of their clothes and ornaments...
262:
...illuminate and brighten all ten directions on both sides in this place.

“So” means that you, being such. “Tūriyagaṇappabodhano” means having the joyful awakening produced by the assembly of divine instruments. “Mahīyamāno” means being honored. “Vajirāvudhoriva” means like the King of Devas (Sakka) who possesses the Vajirāvudha weapon.

He asks: “Others also observe the Uposatha; but what kind of Uposatha did you observe?” “Dhammacariyaṃ” refers to the practice of merit such as giving (dāna). “Vataṃ” means the undertaking of a practice. “Abhirocayi” means: did you delight in and fulfill? There is also a variant reading “Abhirādhayi,” which means: did you accomplish or complete?

The word “Idaṃ” is merely a particle, or it means “this fruit.” “Abhirosase” means you shine transcendently.

When thus questioned by the Great Elder, the deva explained the matter. Therefore, it is said:

That deva, being joyful, when questioned by Moggallāna, answered the problem asked: “This is the fruit of such a deed.”

“One who has conquered the senses, who possesses unfailing effort, who is supreme among men, the noble person named Kassapa, who opens the door to the Deathless (Nibbāna), who is the god above gods, and who is endowed with the marks resulting from a hundred merits.”

“I saw that Great One (Kuñjara), who has crossed the four-fold flood (ogha), and whose appearance is like pure Jambu gold. Having seen that Buddha, I quickly became one with a pure mind; it was only by seeing that Buddha, whose banner is the well-spoken Dhamma (Subhāsitaddhaja).”

“With a detached mind, in my own house strewn with flowers, I offered that pure, exquisite, and flavorful alms-food and robes.”
263:
“By providing the supreme among bipeds, the Blessed Kassapa, with food and drink, robes, snacks, meals, and a place to rest, I, as a son of the gods, rejoice in the celestial city.

By this means, having offered this unobstructed sacrifice, pure in three ways, I abandoned the human body and, like Indra, rejoice in the celestial city.

A wise person who greatly desires long life, beauty, happiness, strength, and a noble appearance, should provide abundant, well-prepared food and drink with a mind free from attachment.

Neither in this world nor in the next does there exist anyone equal or superior to the Buddha. He has reached the state of being the supreme recipient of offerings for those seeking merit and great fruits.”

In those verses, 'Jitindriya' means one who has conquered the senses, with the mind as the sixth, at the foot of the Bodhi tree by the Path of Arahantship, and has thus attained the state of non-indulgence. He is called 'Buddha' because he has fully awakened to the nature of things that should be known, without remainder. He is called 'Anomanikkama' (one of unfailing effort) because of his perfect energy; it means the fulfillment of the fourfold energy and the fourfold Right Effort. 'Naruttama' means the supreme among men, the supreme among bipeds. By the word 'Kassapa', he addresses the Blessed One by his clan name. 'Avāpurantaṃ amatassa dvāraṃ' means opening the Noble Path, which is the gate to the great city of Nibbāna that had been closed since the disappearance of the dispensation of the Blessed Konāgamana. 'Devātideva' means the god beyond all gods. 'Satapuññalakkhaṇa' means one who possesses the marks of a Great Man arising from the power of many hundreds of merits.

'Kuñjara' means one who is like a noble elephant because of subduing the enemies of defilements; it has the same meaning as 'Mahānāga'. He is called 'Oghatiṇṇa' because he has crossed the four floods and the great flood of Saṃsāra.
264:
'Suvaṇṇasiṅgīnada-bimbasādisaṃ' means resembling a statue made of pure Siṅgī gold or Jambunada gold; it means having a complexion like gold. 'Disvā tana khippamahuṃ sucimano' means that upon seeing the Kassapa Buddha, at that very moment of seeing, he became one of pure mind through the power of faith, saying 'The Blessed One is the Fully Enlightened One,' and through the removal of the stains of defilements. This happened quickly just by seeing the Blessed One. 'Subhāsitaddhaja' means one who has the Dhamma as his banner.

'Tamannapānaṃ' refers to the offering of food and drink to that Blessed One. Alternatively, it includes the robe. 'Endowed with taste' means having a delicious and excellent taste; it means sublime. 'Pupphābhikiṇṇamhi' means in a place strewn with flowers, both strung and unstrung, by way of hanging or spreading them out. 'I offered' means I presented or gave. 'Asaṅgamānaso' means with a mind unattached to anything; this is how 'I' should be connected in the sentence.

'Saggaso' means in various heavens by way of repeated rebirths, and even there, in the celestial city of Sudassana. 'Ramāmi' means I play and rejoice.

'Etenupāyena' means by this method, referring to the incomparable gift given to the Blessed Kassapa and his community of disciples during the time he was the Brahmin Gopāla. 'Having offered this unobstructed sacrifice, pure in three ways'—it is called 'unobstructed' (niraggaḷa) because the doors were not closed and it was given with a generous heart; 'three ways' because it was perfected in the three periods of time through the three doors (body, speech, mind) and the methods of doing, causing to do, and recollecting; 'pure' because of the absence of defilements; and 'sacrifice' (yañña) because it was a great gift involving the renunciation of immeasurable wealth. Although that gift was made long ago, because of the nobility of the field (recipient), the object, and the intention, it appears clearly to him as if it were present and nearby when recollected; thus he says 'this'.

Thus, after the son of the gods told his past deeds to the Elder Moggallāna, now wishing to establish others in such prosperity and expressing his supreme faith and reverence for the Tathāgata, he spoke the two verses beginning with 'Āyuñca vaṇṇañca'. In those verses, 'Abhikankhatā' means by one who desires. By the word 'Muni', he addresses the Elder.

By the phrase 'Nayimasmim loke', the son of the gods refers to the world that is visible to him. By 'Parasmim', he refers to the world other than that. By this, in the entire world including the devas...
265:
He shows [this] in the world. In the phrase "there is an equal," let alone being supreme (agga), the meaning is that there is not even an equal (sama). "Āhuneyyānaṃ paramāhutiṃ gato" means that among all those worthy of offerings (āhuneyya) in this world, he has reached the supreme state of being worthy of offerings. There is also a variant reading, "Dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ paramaggataṃ gato," where "paramaggataṃ" means the most supreme state, the state of being the supreme recipient of offerings. For whom has he reached the state of being the supreme recipient? He said, "Puññatthikānaṃ vipulapphalesinaṃ." It is for those who desire merit and long for the great fruits of merit. This shows that the Tathāgata alone is like a fertile field of merit for the world. Some teachers recite it as "Āhuneyyānaṃ paramaggataṃ gato," and the meaning is the same.

Knowing that the deity who was speaking thus had a ready mind, a soft mind, a mind free from hindrances, an uplifted mind, and a confident mind, the Elder revealed the Four Noble Truths. At the conclusion of the teaching of the Truths, that deity was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). Then the Elder returned to the human world and reported the matter to the Blessed One exactly as he and the deity had spoken. The Blessed One made that matter the starting point and preached the Dhamma to the assembled audience. That discourse was beneficial to the great multitude.

## The Explanation of the Mahārathavimāna is finished.
## Thus, the explanation of the meaning of the Fifth Chapter, the Mahāratha Chapter, adorned with fourteen stories, in the Vimānavatthu of the Khuddaka Commentary named Paramatthadīpanī, is finished.
## 6. Pāyāsi Chapter
## 1. Explanation of the First Agāriyavimāna

The story beginning with "Yathā vanaṃ cittalataṃ pabhāsati" is the Agāriyavimāna story. What is its origin? The Blessed One was staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha. At that time, there was a family in Rājagaha where both husband and wife were devoted, endowed with virtue and good conduct, and were like a well (a source of support) for the monks and nuns. Those two spouses, having performed meritorious deeds throughout their lives dedicated to the Triple Gem, passed away and were reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. For them, a golden mansion twelve yojanas in size appeared. There, they enjoyed celestial splendor.
266:
The words beginning with "Athāyasmā Mahāmoggallāno" should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

"Just as the Cittalata Grove, the most excellent garden of the Thirty-three gods, shines,
So too does this mansion of yours stand,
Illuminating the sky.

O deity of great power, possessed of divine psychic power,
What merit did you perform when you were a human being?
By what meritorious deed do you have such shining power,
And why does your radiance illuminate all directions?"
— Thus the Elder asked.

That deity, delighted at being questioned by Moggallāna,
Answered the question as to what deed this was the fruit of:

"When my wife and I were in the human world,
We lived in a house that was like a well [for the Sangha].
With confident minds, we respectfully gave
Abundant gifts of food and drink.

Because of that meritorious deed, I have such radiance...
And my radiance illuminates all directions."

Thus he explained his own prosperity. In the verses, there is nothing new or unusual.

## The Explanation of the First Agāriyavimāna is finished.
267:
## 2. Explanation of the Second Agāriyavimāna

This story beginning with "Yathā vanaṃ cittalataṃ" is the Second Agāriyavimāna story. Here too, the origin is just like the preceding one.

"Just as the Cittalata Grove in the most excellent and praised garden of the Thirty-three gods shines,
So too does this mansion of yours stand illuminating the sky.
O deity of great power, possessed of divine psychic power,
What merit did you perform when you were a human being?
By what meritorious deed do you have such shining power,
And why can your radiance illuminate all directions?"
— Thus [Venerable Moggallāna] asked.

That deity, also being delighted, said, "This fruit is the result of such a meritorious deed" —

"When my wife and I were in the human world, we lived in a house being like a well (a refuge for others).
Having confident minds, we respectfully gave abundant and overflowing gifts of food, snacks, and drinks.
Because of that meritorious deed, I have such radiance... (and so on) ... my radiance can illuminate all directions."

Thus he explained his own prosperity. In the verses, there is no new or special meaning.

## The Explanation of the Second Agāriyavimāna is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Phaladāyakavimāna

This story beginning with "Uccamidaṃ maṇithūṇaṃ" is the Phaladāyakavimāna story. What is the cause and origin of that story? The Blessed One was staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha. At that time, King Bimbisāra had a desire to consume mango fruits out of season. The King said to the gardener, "Friend gardener, a desire to eat mangoes has arisen in me; therefore, [provide] me with mangoes..."
268:
"...bring them and give them to me," he commanded. "Great King, there are no mango fruits on the mango trees. However, if the Great King waits for a short while, I will act so that the mango trees will bear fruit before long," he replied. "Good, fellow, do so," the King said.

The gardener went to the garden, removed the soil from the base of the mango trees, scattered a certain kind of soil, and poured a certain kind of water, so that before long the leaves of the mango trees fell off. Then, he removed that soil, scattered regular soil mixed with phārusaka waste, and watered them well. Soon, the mango trees were filled with buds, tender leaves, and blossoms, and they flowered. Then, young fruits appeared and they bore fruit. Among those mango trees, on one tree, four fruits first developed, golden-yellow like the color of manosilā powder, full of fragrance and flavor, and perfectly ripe.

Taking those fruits, the gardener was going along the way, thinking, "I will present these to the King." Seeing the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna walking for alms, he thought: "These mangoes are the choice first fruits. I will offer these to the Venerable. Let the King kill me or banish me as he wishes. If given to the King, there will be only a small reward of honor in this life. But if given to the Venerable, there will be immeasurable reward both in this life and in the future life." Having thought thus, he offered those fruits to the Elder, went to the King, and reported the matter. Hearing this, the King ordered his men, "Friends, go and investigate whether what this gardener says is true." The Elder offered those fruits to the Blessed One. The Blessed One gave one to the Venerable Sāriputta, one to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, one to the Venerable Mahākassapa, and consumed one himself. The King's men reported this event to the King.

Hearing this, the King, with a joyful heart, said: "This man is truly a firm and wise person; he has sacrificed even his own life to accumulate merit, and he has made his labor fruitful." He then granted the gardener a noble village, clothing, ornaments, and so on as a reward, and said, "Friend gardener, give me a share of the merit you have accumulated by the offering of mango fruits." The gardener replied, "I give it, Great King; take as much of the share of merit as you wish." Later, the gardener passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. For that son of the gods, a mansion appeared, adorned with seven hundred pinnacles, measuring one yojana all around, and having ruby pillars. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna questioned that son of the gods with the verse beginning with "Uccamidaṃ maṇithūṇaṃ":

This mansion of yours with ruby pillars is very high,
Its extent is one yojana all around,
The seven hundred lapis lazuli pillars are extensive and well-distributed,
With delightful golden plates spread over various levels, it has a beautiful ground,
In that mansion you reside,
Fragrant scents blow about,
You partake of pure food,
The sweet sounds of divine songs..."
269:
After the gardener passed away, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. For that son of the gods, a golden mansion appeared, adorned with seven hundred pinnacles and measuring sixteen yojanas in extent. Seeing that mansion, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna questioned him thus:

"This mansion with ruby pillars is very high, measuring sixteen yojanas all around.
Seven hundred pinnacles are extensive, there are pillars of lapis lazuli, and the ground spread with delightful golden plates is very beautiful.

In that mansion you reside, eating and drinking, and the pleasant sounds of divine lutes resonate.
Sixty-four (eight times eight) noble celestial nymphs, well-trained and of beautiful appearance, who delight in Tāvatiṃsa,
Dance, sing, and bring joy.

You have attained divine power and possess great majesty ... (pe) ...
Your radiance illuminates all directions," thus he questioned.

That son of the gods, with a joyful heart ... (pe) ... replied, "This is the fruit of such-and-such a deed."

"The giver of fruit, who gives with a confident mind to those of upright conduct, obtains an abundant reward.
Having gone to heaven, he rejoices in Tāvatiṃsa and experiences the abundant fruit of merit.

O Great Sage, I previously offered four fruits to you.

Therefore, it is truly fitting for a human being seeking happiness, desiring divine bliss, or wishing for human prosperity, to always give fruit."
270:
"Because of that meritorious deed, I have such a complexion... because of that very deed, my complexion shines in all directions," the deva replied to the Venerable Moggallāna.

In that verse, "aṭṭhaṭṭhakā" refers to sixty-four (celestial maidens), with eight in each turret. "Sādhurūpā" means those of excellent nature due to their perfection of form, perfection of moral conduct, and perfection of training. "Dibbā ca kaññā" means celestial maidens. "Tidasacarā" means those who dwell happily in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. "Uḷārā" means those with magnificent wealth.

By the word "phaladāyī," he refers to himself because he had previously given a mango fruit. "Phalaṃ" means the fruit of merit. "Vipulaṃ" means obtaining a great fruit of merit while staying in the human world. "Dadaṃ" means because of the cause of giving. "Ujugatesu" means towards those who have practiced uprightly. "Saggagato" means having reached heaven by way of rebirth, and it implies that "just as I enjoy the vast fruit of merit there in the Tāvatiṃsa realm, so do others."

"Tasmā" means because such prosperity was attained merely by giving four fruits, therefore it is very appropriate (to give). "Niccaṃ" means at all times. "Dibbāni" means the riches belonging to the deva world. "Manussasobhaggataṃ" means reaching a state of splendor among humans. The remaining words are to be understood in the same manner as previously mentioned.

## The Explanation of the Phaladāyaka Vimāna is finished.

## 4. Paṭhama Upassayadāyaka Vimāna Vaṇṇanā

The verse beginning with "Cando yathā vigatavalāhake nabhe" is the Story of the First Giver of Lodging Mansion. What is the origin of this story? The Blessed One was staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha. At that time, a certain monk, having spent the rainy season (Vassa) at a village residence and having performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, was traveling to Rājagaha to pay homage to the Blessed One. In the evening, while on his way, he entered a certain village and, while searching for a place to stay, saw a certain lay follower (upāsaka) and asked, "Lay follower, is there any place suitable for monks to stay in this village?" That lay follower, with a confident mind, went home, consulted with his wife, and...
271:
...having designated a suitable place for the Elder to stay, he prepared a seat there, provided water for washing the feet and a footstool nearby, and invited the Elder in. After the Elder had washed his feet, he lit a lamp, spread coverings on the couch, and offered it. He also invited him for the next day, and on the second day, he fed the Elder and gave a lump of molasses for a drink. He then followed the Elder as he departed and returned. Later, he and his wife passed away and were reborn in a golden mansion twelve yojanas in size in the Tāvatiṃsa realm. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna questioned that deva with two verses:

"Just as the moon in a cloudless sky goes through the atmosphere, shining,
Similarly, this mansion of yours stands in the atmosphere, shining.

O deva of great power, possessed of celestial psychic power, what merit did you perform when you were a human?
Why do you have such blazing power, and why does your complexion shine in all directions?" (Thus he questioned).

The deva replied with these verses:

"That deva, being delighted... this is the fruit of that action."

"When my wife and I were in the human world, we gave a lodging to an Arahant.
With a confident mind, we respectfully gave a vast gift of food and drink.

Because of that meritorious deed, I have such a complexion... and my complexion shines in all directions." (Thus he replied).

In those verses, whatever needs to be said should be understood in the same manner as mentioned below.

## 6. Bhikkhādāyaka Vimāna Vaṇṇanā

The Story of the Alms Giver's Mansion begins with "High is this mansion with pillars of gems." What is the origin of this story? The Blessed One was staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha. At that time, a certain monk on a long journey entered a certain village for alms and stood at the door of a donor's house. In that house, a man who had washed his hands and feet and was sitting down thinking, "I will eat," brought the food near and was putting it into a bowl. Seeing the monk, he poured the food from his bowl into the monk's alms-bowl. Although the monk said, "Give only a portion," he poured it all. The monk, having given words of appreciation (anumodanā), departed. That man, repeatedly reflecting, "I have given food to a hungry monk without eating it myself," attained great rapture and joy (pīti-somanassa). Later, he passed away and was reborn in a golden mansion twelve yojanas in size in the Tāvatiṃsa realm. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, while wandering on a celestial tour, saw that deva shining with great celestial power and questioned him with these verses:
273: "This mansion with jeweled pillars is high, twelve yojanas in extent all around. There are seven hundred magnificent gabled chambers; it is beautiful, being made of beryl pillars and spread with pleasing jeweled slabs. O son of the gods, you have attained divine success and possess great power... and your radiance illuminates all directions." (The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera asked). That son of the gods also replied to the Elder with these verses: "That son of the gods, being delighted... this is the fruit of such a kamma." "When I was a human being among humans, I saw a monk who was thirsty and weary. I gave a single portion of alms-food to that monk; at that time, I provided that monk with a full meal. Because of that kamma, I have such beauty... and my radiance illuminates all directions." (He replied). In that verse, "ekāhaṃ bhikkhaṃ" means I gave just a single portion of alms-food, just the amount of food placed in a single alms-bowl. "Paṭipādayissaṃ" means I gave, I offered. "Samaṅgī bhattena" means I made him endowed with food, having received the alms-food. Thus, when the Great Elder had the son of the gods reveal his own good conduct, he preached the Dhamma to that son of the gods along with his retinue, and then returned to the human world and reported that matter to the Fully Enlightened One. The Teacher, making that the starting point, preached the Dhamma to the assembled crowd. That teaching was beneficial to the great multitude. ## Exposition of the Bhikkhādāyaka Vimāna is finished.
274: ## 7. Yavapālaka-vimānavaṇṇanā (Explanation of the Barley-watcher Mansion) "This high mansion with gem-encrusted pillars" is the Yavapālaka Mansion. What was its origin? The Blessed One was staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha. At that time, a poor boy in Rājagaha was guarding a barley field. One day, having received a barley cake for his breakfast, he thought, "I will go to the field and eat it," and taking the barley cake, he went to the barley field and sat at the foot of a tree. At that moment, an Arahant Thera who was traveling reached that place near mealtime and approached the foot of the tree where the barley-watcher boy was sitting. The barley-watcher boy, looking at the time, asked, "Venerable sir, have you received alms-food?" The Thera remained silent. Realizing that he had not received any, the boy said, "Venerable sir, the time for the meal is near; it is no longer possible to go for alms and eat. Out of compassion for me, please consume this barley cake," and he offered the barley cake to the Thera. The Thera, wishing to favor the boy, consumed the barley cake while the boy was watching, gave a talk of appreciation (anumodanā), and departed. That boy, with a heart full of faith, thinking, "Indeed, I have given well by offering a barley cake to such a noble one," later passed away and was reborn in a mansion in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven according to the method already mentioned. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera questioned that deva with these verses: "This high mansion with gem-encrusted pillars... your radiance also shines in all directions." That deva also replied to the Thera with these verses: "That deva, with a joyful mind... this result is the fruit of such wholesome karma." "When I was a human being among humans, I was a barley-watcher. I saw a monk who was free from defilements, serene, and undisturbed. With a faithful heart, I offered him my own portion of barley cake with my own hands. Having given the offering of barley cake, I now rejoice in the Nandana Grove."
275:
"Because of that meritorious deed, I have such a complexion... My radiance also illuminates all directions," he said. In these verses, there is no new or special meaning.

This story, adorned with the verse beginning with "Alankato malyadharo suvattho," is the Kuṇḍalīvimāna story. What is its origin? The Blessed One was staying at Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī. At that time, the two Chief Disciples, along with their retinue, were wandering through the Kāsi country and reached a certain monastery at sunset. Hearing of their arrival, a certain lay follower living in the village where the monks went for alms approached the elders, paid homage, and offered water for washing their feet, oil for anointing their feet, a couch, a stool, bedding, and a lamp, and invited them for the following day. On the second day, he offered a great gift. The elders, having given him a blessing (anumodanā), departed. Later, that lay follower passed away and was reborn in a golden mansion twelve yojanas in size in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna questioned that deva with these verses:

"With an adorned body, wearing flowers, well-dressed, wearing beautiful earrings, with well-groomed hair and beard;

Wearing bracelets and armlets, possessed of great glory, you shine in your celestial mansion like the moon in the sky.

Celestial lutes of sweet sound also play. Sixty-four well-trained, virtuous, noble celestial maidens who frequent Tāvatiṃsa dance, sing, and bring delight.

You, O deva, have attained divine power and possess great majesty... Your radiance also illuminates all directions." (Thus he questioned.)
276:
That deity also answered the Venerable Mahā Moggallāna with these verses: "That deity, with a joyful heart... this is the fruit of which kamma..."

"When I was a human being among humans, I saw monks who were virtuous, endowed with good conduct, possessed of the three knowledges, the eight knowledges, and the fifteen conducts (vijjā-caraṇa), famous, learned, and who had reached the fruit of Arahantship, which is the destruction of craving. With a faithful heart, I respectfully gave abundant offerings of alms-food, drinks, and excellent gifts."

"Because of that meritorious kamma, such radiance has arisen for me. ... My radiance also illuminates all directions," (he replied).

'Kappitakesamassu' means one with well-groomed hair and beard. 'Āmuttahatthābharaṇo' means one who wears hand ornaments such as rings.

'Taṇhakkhayūpapanna' means those who have reached the fruit of Arahantship, which is the end of craving, or those who have reached and attained Nibbāna by making it their object. The remaining terms are to be understood in the manner already described.
