## 10. Explanation of the (Uttara) Pāyāsi Vimāna

"The Sudhammā hall of the King of Gods" (yā devarājassa sabhā sudhammā) is the Uttara Vimāna story. What is the reason for its origin? After the Blessed One had passed into Parinibbāna and the distribution of the relics had been made, while stupas were being established in various places, and while the great elders headed by Mahā Kassapa, who were selected to recite the Dhamma and Vinaya, as well as other elders, were staying in various places with their respective followings until the commencement of the rains retreat, the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa went to the city of Setabyā with five hundred monks and stayed in the Siṃsapā forest. Then, the Chieftain Pāyāsi, hearing that the elder was staying in that Siṃsapā forest, with a great...
278:
(Chieftain Pāyāsi), surrounded by a large crowd, approached the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa, exchanged pleasantries, and while sitting, declared his own wrong view. Then the elder, demonstrating the existence of the next world by using examples such as the moon and the sun, preached the Pāyāsi Sutta—which is adorned with many reasons and similes, unties the knot of wrong views, and is beautiful in various methods—and established the King in the perfection of right view.

Having become one of pure right view, when giving gifts to recluses, brahmins, the poor, and travelers, because he lacked a grand intention, he gave only coarse things as mere food and clothing: broken rice with sour gruel as the second dish, and hempen garments. Having given gifts in such a disrespectful manner, after the breaking up of the body, he was reborn into a lower state among the companions of the Four Great Kings. However, a young man named Uttara, who was constantly diligent in the King's affairs, was devoted to the giving of gifts. Because he gave gifts respectfully, he was reborn in the host of the Thirty-Three (Tāvatiṃsa). A mansion twelve yojanas in size arose for him. That deity Uttara, wishing to manifest his gratitude, approached the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa together with his mansion, descended from the mansion, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, and stood with joined palms. The elder asked him with these verses:

"Your mansion, which is like the Sudhammā hall of the King of Gods where the assembly of gods meets in harmony, stands illuminating the sky.

O deity, you have attained celestial power and possess great majesty. ... Your radiance illuminates all directions."

That deity, being joyful, replied: "Of what meritorious kamma is this the fruit?"

"Venerable Sir of great majesty, when I was a human being in the human world, I was a young man in the service of King Pāyāsi. Having obtained wealth, I shared and distributed it. Virtuous good people were dear to me. With a faithful heart, I respectfully gave alms-food, drinks, and excellent gifts," he replied.
279: "Because of that meritorious deed, I have such a radiance... (p)... because of that deed, my radiance shines in all directions." The deity answered the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa with these verses. In those verses, "Devarājassa" means of the King of Devas (Sakka). "Sabhā Sudhammā" refers to the assembly hall named Sudhammā. "Yattha" means in which Sudhammā assembly hall. "Acchati" means stays (sits). "Devasaṅgho" refers to the host of Tāvatiṃsa devas. "Samaggo" means assembled in harmony. "Pāyāsissa ahosiṃ māṇavo" means I was once a youth who performed various duties for King Pāyāsi; by name, I was called Uttara. "Saṃvibhāgaṃ akāsiṃ" means I practiced sharing and distributing whatever wealth I obtained as charity, without consuming it myself. "Annañca pānañca pariccajanto" (giving away food and drink) is a supplementary phrase. Alternatively, it means I gave a noble gift; how? respectfully; what kind of object? food and drink—this is how it should be construed. ## The explanation of (Uttara) Pāyāsi Vimāna is finished. ## Thus, the explanation of the meaning of the sixth Pāyāsi Vagga, adorned with ten stories, in the Vimānavatthu Commentary of the Khuddaka Nikāya, called Paramatthadīpanī, is finished. ## 7. ## 3. Maṇithūṇavimānavaṇṇanā

This story, beginning with "Uccamidaṃ maṇithūṇaṃ vimānaṃ," is known as the Maṇithūṇavimāna story. What was the origin of this mansion? The Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī. At that time, many elder monks were living in a forest area. On the road to the village where those monks went for alms, a certain lay follower leveled the uneven ground, removed thorns and obstacles, cleared away bushes and thickets, built bridges over channels during the rainy season, planted shade trees in forest areas, cleared mud from ponds to make them wide and deep, improved the landing places (ghats), gave offerings according to his wealth and means, and observed the moral precepts. Later, when he passed away, he was reborn in a golden mansion twelve yojanas in extent in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approached that deva and questioned him with these verses:

"O deva of great psychic power, this mansion of yours with its gem-encrusted pillars is very high; its extent is twelve yojanas all around.

There are seven hundred magnificent pinnacled houses with pillars of lapis lazuli, spread with beautiful golden mats on various floors, appearing most splendid.

There you dwell, drink divine nectar, and eat divine food; divine lutes also sound with sweet melodies.

In this mansion, there are the five cords of divine sensual pleasure, and celestial maidens whose bodies are covered with golden ornaments are dancing.

Due to what meritorious deed do you have such a complexion? ... and your radiance shines in all directions?"

That deva, being delighted, replied to the elder with these verses: "... this is the fruit of that karma."

"O Bhante of great psychic power, when I was a human being among humans, I built a bridge on a forest path.

I also planted trees for gardens, and I loved the virtuous monks.

With a clear and confident mind, I respectfully gave abundant offerings of food and drink."

"O Bhante of great psychic power, because of that, I have such a complexion, and my radiance shines in all directions," he replied.

In those verses, "vivaṇe ārāmarukkhāni ca" means that in the forest, he had made a park and planted trees there. All the remaining words are as explained previously. The Maṇithūṇavimānavaṇṇanā ends.

## 4. Suvaṇṇavimānavaṇṇanā

'Sovaṇṇamaye pabbatasmim' refers to the Golden Mansion (Suvaṇṇavimāna). What was the origin of this mansion? The Blessed One was staying in the city of Andhakavinda. At that time, a certain lay follower, endowed with faith and devotion and possessed of wealth, had a fragrant chamber (Gandhakuṭi) built on Muṇḍaka Hill near that village. It was complete in every respect and suitable for the Blessed One's residence. While the Blessed One stayed there, the lay follower served Him respectfully. He himself remained established in the perpetual precepts (nicca-sīla) and, having maintained very pure moral restraint, was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven after he passed away. For that deva, a mansion appeared on the peak of a golden mountain, manifesting the power of his meritorious karma, glowing with a net of various jewel rays, surrounded by wonderful terrace railings, beautified with various vast and excellent ornaments, and having well-apportioned walls, pillars, and stairs, delightful with gardens. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, while wandering on a celestial journey, saw that mansion and questioned him with these verses:

"On the peak of the mountain made of gold, there is a mansion that shines in all directions, covered with golden nets and adorned with nets of tinkling bells.

"In that mansion, there are well-crafted eight-sided pillars, all made of lapis lazuli. On each side, seven kinds of jewels are created.

"They are created with lapis lazuli, pure gold, crystal, pure silver, cat's eye gems, pearls, and rubies.

"The ground is wonderful and delightful; no dust rises there. The golden-colored rafters that have been created support the pinnacle."
284:
Four staircases have been created in the four directions; that mansion shines like the young sun with various jewel chambers.

In that mansion, four decorative railings, partitioned and measured in parts, shine brilliantly, illuminating the four directions all around.

In that noble mansion, a deity of great radiance shines exceedingly with his complexion, like the rising sun.

Is this the fruit of your giving, or of your virtue, or of your act of salutation? Being asked, please tell me the reason.

That deity, with a joyful mind, answered Venerable Moggallāna with these verses—

"That deity, with a joyful mind... (answered) this fruit of which kamma."

"Venerable Sir, in the village of Andhakavinda, being filled with faith, I had a monastery built for the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun, performing various tasks with my own hands."

"In that monastery, with a particularly clear mind, I offered scents, flowers, requisites, ointments, and the monastery itself to the Buddha."

"Venerable Sir, because of that meritorious deed, I have obtained this result; I exercise control (enjoy) in this delightful heaven."

"In the delightful garden named Nandana, which is filled with various flocks of birds, I rejoice with dance and song, surrounded by celestial nymphs."

In those verses, 'sabbatopabha' means having radiance that shines from all parts, or emitting radiance. 'Kiṅkiṇijālaka-ppita' means having a net of golden bells attached.

'Sabbe veḷuriyāmayā' means all the pillars are made of cat's-eye gems. Among those pillars, 'ekamekāya aṃsiyā' means on each of the eight facets of the pillars. 'Ratanā satta nimmitā' means created with the seven kinds of jewels; the meaning is that each facet is made of the seven jewels.

With the words beginning with 'veḷūriyasuvaṇṇassa', various jewels are shown. Therein, 'veḷūriyasuvaṇṇassa' means created with cat's-eye gems and gold.
285:
Alternatively, it can be construed as 'citrā' (variegated). Here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental. In the phrase 'phalikā rupiyassa ca', the same method should be understood. 'Masāragallamuttāhi' means with variegated gems (white gems). 'Lohitanga-maṇīhi ca' means with red rubies.

'Na tatthuddhaṃsatī rajo' means that because the floor is made of gems, dust does not rise upwards in that mansion. 'Gopānasīgaṇā' refers to the collection of rafters. 'Pītā' means yellow in color, being made of gold or gems such as topaz. 'Kūṭaṃ dhārenti' means they support the pinnacle (summit) made of the seven jewels.

1138-9. 'Nānāratanagabbhehi' means with chambers made of various jewels. 'Vediyā' refers to the railings (vedikā). 'Catasso' means four (four railings) in the four directions. Therefore, it is said, 'samantā caturo disā' (all around the four directions).

'Mahappabho' means having great radiance. 'Udayanto' means rising. 'Bhāṇumā' refers to the sun.

'Tena' means because of that aforementioned meritorious deed which is the cause. 'Mayhaṃ' means by me (mayā). 'Idaṃ' refers to this fruit of merit, or this divine sovereignty. Therefore, it is said, 'vasaṃ vattemi' (I exercise control).

'Nandane' means in this heaven which is the place of arising for delightful divine prosperity; specifically there, in the delightful Nandana grove. The construction is: 'I rejoice in this delightful Nandana grove.' The rest is exactly as previously explained.

When the deity had thus revealed his own meritorious deed, the Elder preached the Dhamma to that deity along with his retinue and then reported the matter to the Blessed One. ## 5. Commentary on the Amba Vimāna (Amba-vimāna-vaṇṇanā)

This story of the mansion beginning with "Uccamidaṃ maṇithūṇaṃ" is the Amba Vimāna story. What is its origin? The Blessed One was staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha. At that time, in Rājagaha, a certain poor man, who worked as a hired laborer for others in exchange for food and wages, was guarding a mango grove.

One day, that man saw the Venerable Sāriputta walking along the road near that mango grove, his body drenched in sweat, on a ground scorched by the sun's heat, oppressed by the hot sand, and covered by shimmering waves of mirage. Seeing him, he felt deep respect and great esteem, approached him, and said: "Venerable sir, this summer heat is very intense. You appear to be extremely exhausted. Venerable sir, please, out of compassion for me, enter this mango grove, rest for a moment, and proceed after dispelling the fatigue of your journey." The Elder, wishing to especially increase the man's faith, entered the grove and sat at the foot of a certain mango tree.

Again, the man said: "Venerable sir, if you wish to bathe, I will draw water from this well and bathe you, and I will also offer you drinking water." The Elder accepted by remaining silent. The man drew water from the well, filtered it, and bathed the Elder. After bathing him, he washed the Elder's hands and feet and offered drinking water to the seated Elder. After drinking the water and his fatigue being relieved, the Elder spoke words of appreciation (anumodanā) to the man for the gift of water and the bathing, and then departed.

Then the man experienced sublime joy and happiness, thinking: "Indeed, I have relieved the heat of the Elder who was scorched by the sun! Indeed, I have accumulated much merit!" Later, he passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approached him and asked about the merit he had performed with these verses:

"This mansion with jeweled pillars is high, twelve leagues all around. There are seven hundred magnificent gabled houses, with beautiful pillars of lapis lazuli, spread with delightful floorings."
287:
'There you stay, drink, and eat; and divine lutes sound melodiously. In this mansion, there are the five divine strands of sensual pleasure, and goddesses adorned in gold ornaments are dancing. By what kind of merit do you have such a complexion? ... And your radiance shines in all directions?' (Thus asked the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna).

That deva, with a delighted mind (to answer the question asked by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna), replied: '...This is the fruit of such a meritorious deed.'

In the month of Āsāḷha, the last month of summer, while the sun was shining with intense heat, a man who was a hired laborer for others was watering a mango grove.

Then a monk known as Sāriputta, who was weary in body but not weary in mind, came along that way.

Seeing that venerable one approaching, I, the waterer of the mango grove, said: "Venerable sir, it is well; let me bathe you. Such bathing will bring me happiness."

Out of compassion for me, that venerable one laid down his bowl and robes and sat in the shade at the foot of a tree, wearing only a single robe.

With a clear mind, that man bathed the venerable one, who was sitting in the shade at the foot of the tree in a single robe, with pure water.

Thinking, "The mango tree has been watered, the monk has been bathed, and I have accumulated no small amount of merit," that man pervaded his entire body with joy and rapture.

In that life, I performed only that much meritorious deed. Having abandoned the human body, I have arrived at the Nandana Grove.'
288:
"In the delightful Nandana Grove, filled with various flocks of birds, I rejoice with dance and song, surrounded by celestial nymphs." Thus the deva also explained to the Elder with these verses.

In those verses, "gimhānaṃ pacchime māse" means in the month of Āsāḷha. "Patapante" means shining extremely brightly, emitting heat in every way. "Divankare" means the sun; or this is simply the reading. "Asiñcati" means he waters; the 'a' is merely a particle; it means he constantly performs the pouring of water at the roots of the mango trees. There is also a reading "asiñcatha," meaning he watered. Some also read "asiñcahaṃ," meaning "being a hired laborer for others, I then watered the mango grove."

"Tena" means he went towards the direction where that mango grove was located. "Akilantova cetasā" means that since mental suffering had been abandoned by the Path itself, although he was not weary in mind, he was weary in body; thus it should be connected that he went by that road.

1153-4. It should be connected as: "I, being the waterer of the mangoes at that time, spoke." "Ekacīvaro" means having only a single robe because of the desire to bathe.

"Iti" means in this way: "The mango tree has been watered, the monk has been bathed, and I have accumulated no small amount of merit; three benefits have been achieved with a single effort." It should be connected that with the joy arising in this manner, that man pervades his entire body, making it completely filled without interval. Here, the present tense is used in the sense of the past, meaning "he pervaded."

"Tadav ettakaṃ kammaṃ" means "I performed only that much deed, merely the gift of water; I do not remember any other (merit) in that life." The rest is just as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Amba Vimāna is finished.
289:
## 6. Gopālavimānavaṇṇanā

The story presented with the verse beginning with "Disvāna devaṃ paṭipucchi bhikkhu" is the Gopālavimāna Story. What is its origin? The Blessed One was staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha. At that time, a certain cowherd living in Rājagaha took a bundle of barley cakes (kummāsa) tied with a rag for his breakfast and left the city for the pasture where the cows graze.

Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, knowing that "This cowherd will die this very moment, and by giving me the barley cakes, he will be reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven," went near him. Seeing that it was time for the monk's meal, the cowherd felt a desire to offer the barley cakes to the Elder. At that moment, the cows entered a field of beans. Then the cowherd thought, "Should I offer the barley cakes to the Elder, or should I drive the cows out of the bean field?" Then it occurred to him, "Let the owners of the bean field do to me as they wish; if the Elder leaves, there might be an obstacle to my offering of barley cakes. Let me first offer the barley cakes to the Venerable One." Having thought so, he offered the barley cakes to the Elder. Out of compassion, the Elder accepted them.

Then, while the cowherd was running fast to turn the cows back, without regard for danger, he stepped on a highly venomous snake, which bit him. The Elder, out of compassion for him, began to eat the barley cakes. The cowherd, having turned the cows back and returned, saw the Elder eating the barley cakes. With a confident heart and experiencing great joy and happiness, he sat down. At that very moment, the poison spread throughout his entire body. In an instant, the force of the poison reached the top of his head, and he passed away. After passing away, he was reborn in a golden mansion twelve yojanas in size in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, seeing that son of the gods, questioned him with these verses:

Seeing the son of the gods, the monk questioned him: In the lofty and long-lasting mansion,
Adorned with hand-ornaments, famous, you shine in the celestial mansion like the moon in the sky.
290:
Adorned, wearing garlands, well-dressed, with beautiful earrings, hair and beard well-groomed, wearing hand-ornaments, famous, you shine in the celestial mansion like the moon-mansion in the sky.

Celestial lutes of pleasant sound also play. Sixty-four well-trained, good-natured, noble celestial maidens, who dwell happily in Tāvatiṃsa, dance, sing, and gladden the heart. You have attained celestial success and possess great power... Your radiance illuminates all directions.

That son of the gods also answered Venerable Mahāmoggallāna thus: "That son of the gods, with a delighted heart... this is the fruit of that wholesome deed."

"When I was a human being among humans, I used to gather and look after the cows of others. Then a monk came near me. The cows went into a bean field to eat."

"Venerable Sir, today there were two tasks, and both had to be done; thus I thought at that time. Then, with wise reflection, I remembered and saying, 'Venerable Sir, I offer this,' I threw down the cloth containing the barley cakes."

"I quickly went down to the bean field before this herd of cows could destroy the field, which is the property of the owner. Then a black snake of intense venom bit my foot as I was going in haste."

"I reached a state of suffering and was severely oppressed. That monk, having himself untied the bundle of barley cakes, ate them out of compassion for me. Having passed away from that human life, I became a son of the gods."
291:
"I performed that faultless wholesome deed myself. I am experiencing the fruit of the wholesome deed which is the cause of happiness. Venerable Sir, you have been very compassionate toward me. With a heart of gratitude, I pay homage to you.

In the world including the devas, there is no other sage (muni) as compassionate as you. Venerable Sir, you have been very compassionate toward me. With a heart of gratitude, I pay homage to you.

Whether in this world or the next, there is no other sage as compassionate as you. Venerable Sir, you have been very compassionate toward me. With a heart of gratitude, I pay homage to you," he said.

Then Venerable Mahāmoggallāna reported the matter to the Blessed One exactly as he and the son of the gods had spoken. The Blessed One, confirming the matter and taking that occurrence as the starting point, spoke the verses beginning with "Disvāna devaṃ paṭipucchi bhikkhu" to teach the Dhamma to the assembled audience.

In those verses, "devaṃ" refers to the Gopāla son of the gods. "Bhikkhū" refers to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, as spoken by the Blessed One. He is called a bhikkhu because he has completely destroyed all defilements. Because the mansion lasts for a long time or for an entire aeon (kappa), it is called "ciraṭṭhitike." Some teachers also read it as "ciraṭṭhitikaṃ." That term should be connected with the word "devaṃ." That son of the gods also deserves to be called "ciraṭṭhitike" because he stays in that mansion for over thirty-six million years. "Yathāpi candimā" means just as the moon-god (Candimā devaputta) shines in his celestial mansion, radiant with a mass of pleasant, cool, and delightful rays; the remaining words should be understood as "shining in the same way."

"Alaṅkato" and the following words show the manner in which the Elder questioned the son of the gods, and their meaning is exactly as stated previously.
292:
Saṅgammā means having gathered or because of gathering. Here, the causal sense is also included, meaning because many cattle have become one. Āgā means came. Māse refers to crops such as kidney beans.

Dvayañja means there are two tasks to be done at this time. The phrase "ubhayañca kāriyaṃ" is a synonymous expression for the meaning already stated. Saññaṃ refers to the perception associated with the Dhamma. Therefore, it is said "yoniso" (wisely). Paṭiladdhā means having obtained. Khipim means I dropped or placed in the hand by way of causing to receive. Anantakaṃ is a piece of cloth in which boiled barley is placed and tied; here, the letter "a" is merely an expletive particle.

So means that I. Turito means hurriedly or in a flurry. Avāsariṃ means I approached or entered. The phrase "purā ayaṃ bhañjati yassidaṃ dhanaṃ" means before this herd of cattle destroys this property, which is the kidney bean crop of that field owner, even before they trample and destroy it. Tato means in that place. "Turitassa me sato" means while I was in a hurry, having gone quickly on the path without looking at the cobra.

"Aṭṭomhi dukkhena pīḷito" means I am afflicted, oppressed, and troubled by the suffering of death due to that snakebite. Ahāsī means swallowed or consumed. "Tato cuto kālakatomhi devatā" means having passed away from that human existence and reached death, or having done the time which is the exhaustion of the life-force in that human existence, immediately after that death, I became a deity by attaining the state of a deva.

Tayā means there is no other sage (muni) or seer (isi) endowed with the qualities of a sage like you. Or, this word tayā is a word in the instrumental case used in the sense of the ablative. The remaining words are to be understood in the manner already stated.

## The Explanation of the Gopāla Mansion is finished.
293:
## 7. Explanation of the Kaṇṭhaka Mansion

The story beginning with "Puṇṇamāse yathā cando" is the Story of the Kaṇṭhaka Mansion. What is the origin of this story? The Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī. At that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, while wandering for alms among the devas in the manner previously described, arrived at the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. At that moment, the young deva Kaṇṭhaka came out of his own mansion, mounted a divine vehicle, and was going to the park with a large retinue and great divine power. Seeing the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, he was filled with great respect and reverence, quickly descended from the vehicle, approached the Elder, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, and stood with his hands raised in salutation (añjali) to his head. Then the Elder asked that young deva:

"Just as on a full moon day, the moon, the lord of the stars, surrounded by the host of stars, constantly revolves all around.

Similar to that moon, this divine mansion in the city of the devas also shines exceedingly with its splendor, like the rising sun.

(It is made) of beryl, gold, crystal, silver, masāragalla (cat's eye), pearls, and red precious stones.

The ground, spread with beryl, is variegated and delightful to the heart. Your palace, complete with beautiful and pleasant gabled houses, is well-constructed.

Your lotus ponds are delightful, frequented by many fish, with clear and transparent water, and spread with golden sand.

Covered with various kinds of lotuses and spread with white lotuses (puṇḍarīka), those ponds diffuse a pleasant fragrance when stirred by the wind.

On both sides of that pond, groves of trees are well-created, endowed with both flowering trees and fruit trees.

As you sit on a couch with golden legs, spread with soft woolen rugs, celestial nymphs attend to you like the king of devas."
294:
"Celestial nymphs, covered with all kinds of ornaments and decorated with various garlands, delight you who possess great power; you rejoice like the Deva King Vasavattī.

Endowed with delight, you rejoice in the sounds of drums, conchs, kettledrums, lutes, and small drums, and in well-performed dance and song.

You have various divine forms, divine sounds, and also tastes, fragrances that you desire, and heart-delighting touches.

O young deva of great splendor, in that noble mansion, you shine exceedingly with your beauty, like the rising sun.

Is this the fruit of your giving (dāna), or of your virtue (sīla), or of your act of salutation (añjali)? Being asked by me, please tell me that."

The Venerable Moggallāna asked about the meritorious deed performed by way of praising the attained prosperity.

That young deva, being delighted and asked by Moggallāna, explained the problem when questioned as to what meritorious deed this was the fruit of:

"In the city of Kapilavatthu, the best of the cities of the Sakyans, I was the horse named Kaṇṭhaka, co-natal with the son of King Suddhodana.

When he went forth at midnight for the sake of Awakening, that Bodhisatta, with his soft hands and with his very red nails like a net—

Having patted my thigh, said: 'Carry me, friend. Having attained the supreme Perfect Enlightenment, I shall save the world.'

When I heard those words, great joy arose in me. At that time, with an uplifted and happy mind, I neighed.

Knowing that the Sakyan prince of great fame had mounted me, with an uplifted and joyful mind, I carried that Best of Men."
295:
“Having reached the territory of others, when the sun had risen, that Great Man abandoned me and the minister Channa, and departed without any lingering attachment.

“I licked his feet, which had copper-colored nails, with my tongue; and as that Great Hero (Mahāvīra) departed, I watched him while weeping.

“Because I could no longer see that glorious Prince of the Sakyans, a severe illness came upon me, and my death occurred quickly.

“By the power of that very devotion, I now dwell in this celestial mansion, endowed with all the five cords of sensual pleasure, like a god in the city of gods.

“The joy I felt upon hearing the voice of the Bodhisatta—by that very root of merit, I shall reach the destruction of the taints (āsavas).

“Venerable sir, if you should go to the presence of the Teacher, the Buddha, please convey my salutation, saying with my words that I pay homage to him with my head.

“I too shall go to see the Conqueror (Jina), the peerless individual; for it is rare to see such Lords of the World (Lokanātha), the Steadfast Ones.” (Thus he spoke).

That deity also spoke of the meritorious deed he had performed. In his immediately preceding life, this deity was the king of horses named Kanthaka, who was born at the same time as our Bodhisatta. At the time of the Great Renunciation, he was ridden [by the Bodhisatta], and in the remainder of that night, he crossed three kingdoms and brought the Great Man to the bank of the Anoma River. Then, when the sun rose, the Great Being (Mahāsatta) took the bowl and robes offered by Ghaṭīkāra Mahābrahmā, ordained as a monk, and sent [Kanthaka] back toward the city of Kapilavatthu along with the minister Channa. With a heart heavy with affection, that king of horses licked the feet of the Great Man with his tongue, opened his clear and gentle eyes, and watched as far as his sight could reach. When the Lord of the World (Lokanātha) passed beyond the range of his vision, he thought with a devoted mind, “I have carried such a Great Man, the Foremost Leader of the World (Lokagganāyaka); indeed, my body has been fruitful!” Unable to bear the suffering of separation due to the power of the love from their long association, and being urged by the nature of the impending divine bliss, he died and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Referring to that event, [the Buddha] spoke the verse beginning with “Puṇṇamāse yathā cando”. In those verses, “Puṇṇamāse” means on the full moon day, on the fifteenth day of the waxing moon...
296:
(Due to the power of the love from their long association [with the Bodhisatta], and being urged by the nature of the impending divine bliss, he passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Referring to that event, it was said: “As the moon on the full moon day... I was in Kapilavatthu,” and so on.

In that context, “Puṇṇamāse” means on the full moon day, on the fifteenth day of the waxing moon. “Tārakādhipati” means the lord of the stars. “Sasī” means the moon which has the mark of a rabbit. Some teachers recite “Tārakādhipa dissati”; in their view, “Tārakādhipā” is a designation without a case ending, and the construction should be understood as “appearing as the lord of the stars, it revolves.”

“Dibbaṃ devapuramhi ca” means divine even in the city of gods. Just as the city of gods is superior to the dwelling place of humans, this shows that your celestial mansion is even more excellent than the city of gods. Therefore, it is said, “It shines exceedingly with color like the rising sun,” meaning it is like the sun when it is rising.

“Veḷūriyasuvaṇṇassa”: this construction should be understood with the remaining words as “this mansion is created with beryl and pure gold.” “Phalikā” means with crystal gems.

“Pokkharaṇီ” means lotus ponds.

1177-8. “Tassā” means of that lotus pond. “Vanagumbā” refers to the flowering shrubs in the garden. “Devarājaṃ vā” means like the King of the Gods (Sakka). “Upatiṭṭhanti” means they perform attendance/service.

“Sabbābharaṇasañchannā” means covered with all the ornaments of goddesses, meaning those whose bodies are fully adorned. “Vasavattီ vā” means like the King of Gods, Vasavatti.

“Bherisaṅkhamudiṅgāhi”: this is spoken with a change of gender, and the construction should be understood as “with large drums, with conchs, and with mudiṅga drums.” “Ratisampanno” means being endowed with divine delight. “Naccagီte suvādite” means either “in dancing, singing, and well-played music” or “because dancing, singing, and well-played music are the causal signs.” Here, the locative case is in the sense of a cause (nimitta). Alternatively, the remaining word “pavattite” (produced/set in motion) should be added and understood.

“Divvā te vividhā rūpā” means the various kinds of forms (sights) belonging to the heavenly realm, cognizable by the eye, which are as you desire, pleasing to the mind... (the verb should be connected accordingly). In the phrases “Divvā saddādီsu” and so on, it should be understood in this same manner.)
297:
The word *vijjanti* (exist) should be brought in and connected to mean 'there are delightful sights.' The same method should be understood for terms such as *dibbā saddā* (divine sounds) and others.

In the phrase *kaṇḍako sahajo ahaṃ*, the word *ahaṃ* is merely a particle. Some teachers read it as *ahu*. The meaning is that the king of horses named Kaṇḍaka was 'co-born' (*sahaja*) because he was born on the same day as the Great Being (the Bodhisatta).

*Aḍḍharattāya* means at midnight, during the time of the middle watch (*majjhimayāma*). In the phrase *bodhāya mabhinikkhami*, the letter 'm' is a euphonic junction (*padasandhi*). The meaning is that he went forth on the Great Departure for the sake of realizing the Four Noble Truths. By the phrase *mudūhi pāṇīhi*, it refers to the mark of a Great Man having soft palms. *Jālitambanakhehi* means with fingers like a net and very red nails. By this, he shows the Great Man's mark of having netted hands and the secondary characteristic (*anubyañjana*) of having copper-colored nails.

*Satthi* refers to the horse's knee; however, in this context, the thigh area (*ūruppadesa*) near the knee is called *satthi*. *Ākoṭayitvāna* means having patted or struck. *Vaha sammā* means 'Friend Kaṇḍaka, carry me for this one night; be my state steed.' The Great Being then showed the purpose of being carried, saying, 'I, having reached supreme Enlightenment, shall deliver the world.' By this, he shows the incomparable nature of the journey's purpose: 'I, having attained the supreme, unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment, will deliver the world including the devas from the great flood of saṃsāra; therefore, do not think of this journey as just any ordinary journey.'

1188-9. *Hāsa* means joy. *Vipula* means great and extensive. *Abhisīsiṃ* means I accepted or acknowledged. By the words *abhirūḷhañca maṃ ñatvā sakyaputtaṃ mahāyasaṃ*, it means 'knowing that I, the Sakyan prince of great fame and extensive retinue, the Great Being, was seated upon [him].' *Vahissaṃ* means 'I carried [him].'

1190-91. *Paresaṃ* means 'of other kings.' *Vijitaṃ* means 'foreign territory.' *Ohāya* means 'having abandoned.' *Apakkami* means 'he began to depart.' Some also read it as *paribbaji*. *Parilehissaṃ* means 'I licked all around.' *Udikkhissaṃ* means 'I gazed upon.'
298:
1192-3. *Garukābādhaṃ* means a heavy and severe illness, a suffering ending in death. Therefore, it was said, 'Death came quickly to me.' That horse Kaṇḍaka had firm devotion to the Great Being over many lifetimes, so he could not bear the pain of separation. However, when he heard, 'He has gone forth to attain Supreme Enlightenment,' a vast spiritual joy and gladness (*nirāmisa pītisomanassa*) arose. By the power of that wholesome deed of faith, after death, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, and great divine splendors appeared for him. Thus it is said, 'By the power of that very [devotion],' meaning by the strength of the merit consisting of faith that reached its object. He became like Sakka, the king of devas, in the celestial mansion of Tāvatiṃsa.

'Hearing the sound of Enlightenment, joy arose in me' means when he first heard the word 'Enlightenment' in the phrase 'He has reached supreme Enlightenment,' joy arose in him then. By that very root of merit, that very seed of merit which is the cause of joy, 'I shall touch/reach [Nibbāna].'

Thus, the deva, having spoken of his own wholesome kamma which was the cause of his attained and future success in life, now wished to go to the Blessed One himself, but first desired to send his salutation to the Teacher through the Elder. He spoke the verse beginning with *Sace*. In that verse, *sace gaccheyyāsi* means 'if you should go.' Some read *sace gacchasi*, but the meaning is the same. *Mama pi naṃ vacanena* should be connected as: 'Not only of your own accord, but also with my words, please speak to the Blessed One; say that I too pay homage with my head.'

To show that although he sends a salutation now, he will not stop at just sending it, he said, 'I too will go to see the Victor (*Jina*), the peerless person.' To show the very firm reason for going, he said, 'It is difficult to see such Lords of the World (*Lokanātha*).'

'That Kaṇḍaka, being grateful and appreciative, approached the Teacher. Having heard the words of the One with Vision, he purified the Eye of Dhamma.

Having purified wrong view, doubt, and rites and rituals, and having paid homage to the Teacher's feet, he disappeared right there.'

These two verses were placed by the Recorders of the Council (*Saṅgီtikāras*). In those verses, 'having heard the words of the One with Vision' means having heard the words of the Blessed One who possesses the five types of eyes of wisdom, he attained the 'Eye of Dhamma,' which is the Knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry (*Sotāpattimagga-ñāṇa*). Attaining that Path-knowledge is itself called 'purifying.' 'Having purified wrong view' should be connected with 'by completely cutting off wrong view, and by purifying doubt regarding the seven or eight objects, and rites and rituals (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*) which are the belief that one is purified by mere practices.' The false graspings that arose together with the causes for that deva are called *vatāni*. The remaining words are as explained before.
299:
In that verse, 'sutvā giraṃ cakkhumato' means having heard the words of the Fully Enlightened One, who is endowed with the five kinds of eyes. 'Dhamma-cakkhu' (the Eye of Dhamma) refers to the knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpattimagga). 'Visodhayi' means he attained it. Indeed, the attainment of that Path of Stream-entry is itself called 'purification.'

'Visodhetvā diṭṭhigataṃ' means having completely eradicated wrong views. 'Vicikicchaṃ vatāni ca' should be interpreted as having purified and abandoned the sixteen types of doubt and the eight types of doubt, as well as 'sīlabbataparāmāsa'—the clinging to rites and rituals that arises with the thought, "One is purified through rites and rituals." For that deva, the various types of wrong grasping (parāmāsa) that arise are called 'vatāni.' The remaining words are to be understood in the same way as previously explained.

## The Description of Kaṇḍakavimāna is finished.

## 8. Anekavaṇṇavimānavaṇṇanā

The verse beginning with 'Anekavaṇṇaṃ darasokanāsanaṃ' is the Anekavaṇṇavimāna story. What is its origin? It was when the Blessed One was staying at Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī. At that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, while wandering through the celestial realms as mentioned above, arrived at the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Then, the deva Anekavaṇṇa, seeing the elder, felt great respect and reverence, approached him, and stood with his hands joined in salutation. The elder questioned him thus:

"Having ascended the mansion of many colors, which destroys distress and grief, and is of various wonders;
Surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs, you rejoice like Sunimmita, the lord of devas.

There is no one equal to you in retinue, merit, or psychic power; how then could there be anyone superior?
All the devas of the Tāvatiṃsa host assemble and pay homage to you, just as the devas worship the moon.

These celestial nymphs also surround you, bringing delight through dancing and singing."
300: 'You have attained celestial power and possess great majesty. What merit did you perform when you were a human? Why do you have such radiant majesty, and your splendor illuminates all directions?' (Thus he asked). He asked about the kamma performed by way of praising the attained prosperity. To show that matter, it is said: 'That deity, being delighted... this is the fruit of that kamma.' He also said: 'Venerable Sir, in the past I was a disciple of the Conqueror named Sumedha. I was a worldling (puthujjana), not yet having realized the truths. I lived as a monk for seven years. Having paid homage at the jewel stupa covered with a golden net of the Teacher, the Conqueror Sumedha, who had crossed the flood, who was such a one, and who had attained Parinibbāna, I gained confidence in my mind. I had no gift, nor did I have anything to give, but I encouraged others there: "Worship the relics of the one worthy of worship; by doing so, you will go from here to heaven." I performed only that wholesome kamma, and I myself enjoy celestial happiness. I rejoice in the midst of the Tāvatiṃsa host, and I have not yet reached the exhaustion of that merit.' It is said that thirty thousand aeons ago, the Fully Enlightened One named Sumedha appeared in the world. Having illuminated the world including the devas with a single radiance and having performed the duties of a Buddha, he attained Parinibbāna. When people took the relics of the Blessed One and built a jewel stupa, a certain man ordained in the Teacher's dispensation and for seven years...
301:
After the Parinibbāna of the Buddha, while the relics were being taken and a jewel stupa was being erected for worship, a certain man went forth as a monk in the Dispensation and practiced the sublime life for seven years. However, due to an unsettled mind, he became filled with remorse and disrobed. Even after disrobing, because of a great sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and a desire for the Dhamma, he spent his time wandering about, sweeping the stupa courtyard, performing tasks such as plastering the ground, observing the constant precepts (nicca-sīla) and the Uposatha precepts, listening to the Dhamma, and encouraging others to perform meritorious deeds. When he passed away at the end of his life, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Due to the greatness of his meritorious karma, that son of the gods possessed great power and majesty, and being honored and worshipped by the deities such as Sakka, he remained there for the full life span. After passing away from there, he wandered repeatedly through the realms of gods and humans, and in the time of this present Buddha, due to the remaining fruit of that same karma, he was reborn again in the Tāvatiṃsa abode. The deities recognized him as "Anekavaṇṇa" (Of Many Colors). With reference to this, it was said: "Then the son of the gods Anekavaṇṇa... (pe)... spoke of how he had not reached the end of that merit."

In that verse, "Anekavaṇṇa" means having various colors due to the power of blue, yellow, and so on, and also having various forms due to the diverse shapes of the nearby mansions and such. "Darasokanāsana" means the destroyer of distress and sorrow because it dispels distress and feverish longing through its coolness, and because there is no room for sorrow due to its pleasantness and beauty. "Anekacitta" means having various wonderful appearances. "Sunimmito bhūtapatīva" means that although he was born among the assembly of Tāvatiṃsa, because of his extensive divine bliss, he rejoices, is pleased, and delights like the divine king Sunimmita.

"Samassamo" means being equal to those who are equal. There is no one equal to you in terms of being peerless; if so, for what reason could there be anyone superior or greater than you? As to what makes one equal or superior, he said: "By retinue, merit, and psychic power." There, "yasena" means by retinue. "Iddhiyā" means by majesty. Alternatively, "yasena" is by sovereignty, and "iddhiyā" is by divine power. Alternatively, "yasena" is by the attainment of wealth, and "iddhiyā" is by the fulfillment of desired sensual pleasures. Alternatively, "yasena" is by fame and renown, and "iddhiyā" is by prosperity. "Puññena" means by the fruit of the merit mentioned in various places, or by the meritorious karma itself.

The meaning taken generally as "sabbe ca devā" (and all the gods) is specifically stated by the word "tidasagaṇā" (the groups of the Thirty-three). Although they may pay respect to some individuals, they do not do so with joy...
302:
...they do not do so; it is not like that for him. To show that they do so even with joy for him, it is said: "samacca" (having assembled).

"Taṃ" means "you." "Sasiṃva devā" means that just as humans and gods, filled with reverence, worship the moon marked with the hare seen on the first day of the waxing moon, in the same way, all the groups of the Thirty-three worship you.

By the word "bhadante," he addresses the Elder with great respect and esteem. "Ahu vāsiṃ" means "I was." "Pubbe" means "in a previous life." "Sumedhanāmassa jinassa sāvako" means being a disciple by way of having gone forth in the Dispensation of the Fully Enlightened Buddha who was well-known by the name Sumedha. "Puthujjano" means one who is not an Ariya (a worldling). Even in that state of being a monk, he was "ananubodho" (without realization) because of the absence of even a mere realization of the Truths. "So satta vassāni paribbajissahaṃ" means "I wandered for seven years with only the virtue of the monkhood, but I did not attain any superhuman states such as jhāna, path, or fruit."

"Ratanuccayaṃ" refers to a high jewel stupa raised with gems, gold, and so forth. "Hemajālena channaṃ" means covered all around and above with a golden net. "Vanditvā" means having paid homage at various places with the fivefold prostration. "Thūpasmiṃ manaṃ pasādayiံ" means "I inspired my mind at the stupa, thinking, 'This stupa is indeed for the relics which are the basis of the qualities of the All-Knowing One.'"

"Na māsi dānaṃ" means "there was no gift given by me." Why? "Na ca metthi dātuṃ" means "I had nothing belonging to me to give as a gift; no gift-object existed." However, I did encourage other beings in that giving. They also read "Paresañca tattha samādapesiံ"; there, the word "paresaṃ" should be understood as having the sense of the accusative case although it is in the genitive form. The words beginning with "pūjetha naṃ" (worship it) show the manner of encouragement, and it should be connected as "worship that relic." In the phrase "evaṃ kira," the word "kira" expresses hearsay or tradition.

"Na tassa puññassa khayampi ajjhagā" means that he did not reach the exhaustion of the meritorious karma performed at that time dedicated to the Blessed One Sumedha, and it shows that he is still experiencing the remaining fruit of that same karma. What is not stated here should be understood as being easily known according to the method stated below.

## The explanation of the Anekavaṇṇavimāna is finished.
303:
## 9. Maṭṭhakuṇḍalīvimānavaṇṇanā

This Vimāna story beginning with 'Alaṅkato Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī' is the Maṭṭhakuṇḍalīvimāna. What is the origin of this story? The Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana monastery in Sāvatthī. At that time, there lived in Sāvatthī a Brahmin named Adinnapubbaka. Although this Brahmin was wealthy, possessing great riches and many belongings, he was without faith, without devotion, and held wrong views. He would not give anything to anyone. Because of his habit of never giving, he was well-known as 'Adinnapubbaka' (One who has never given before).

Due to his wrong views and stinginess, he did not even wish to see the Blessed One or the Blessed One's disciples. He instructed his only son, named Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī: 'Dear son, you must not approach or see the ascetic Gotama and his disciples.' The son did as his father commanded. While living in this manner, the son, Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, fell ill. The Brahmin did not provide medical treatment because he feared the loss of his wealth. Only when the illness worsened did he call for physicians to see him. After examining the youth's body, the physicians realized, 'He is incurable,' and departed. The Brahmin thought, 'If he dies inside the house, it will be a painful task to carry him out,' and so he had his son lie down outside on the front porch.

At the time of dawn, the Blessed One, having arisen from the attainment of great compassion (mahākaruṇāsamāpatti) and surveying the world, saw the youth Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, whose life span was exhausted and who was to pass away that very day, and whose karma leading to hell was finding its opportunity. The Blessed One thought: 'If I go there, this youth will gain faith in me and be reborn in the celestial realm. Then, he will approach his father who is weeping at the cemetery and cause him to feel spiritual urgency (saṃvega). In this way, both the father and the son will come to me. A great multitude of people will also assemble. When I teach the Dhamma at that assembly, many will realize the Four Noble Truths.' Having known this, in the morning, he adjusted his lower robe, took his bowl and robes, and entered Sāvatthī for alms together with a large community of monks. Standing near the house of Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī's father, he emitted the six-colored Buddha-rays.

Upon seeing those rays, the youth wondered, 'What is this light?' and looking here and there, he saw the Blessed One, who was composed, guarded, with peaceful faculties, shining with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor characteristics, the fathom-wide aura, and the crest-light (ketumālā), resplendent with incomparable Buddha-glory and inconceivable Buddha-power. Seeing this, the youth thought: 'This venerable one, endowed with such physical perfection, who surpasses the sun with his own radiance and the moon with his pleasing appearance, must surely be the Blessed One who has arrived here.'
304:
He surpasses all ascetics and Brahmins with his serenity. 'Serenity itself must surely reside in this Blessed One; I think he is the supreme person in this world, and he has come here solely out of compassion for me.' With his entire body constantly suffused with joy centered on the Buddha, experiencing immeasurable rapture and happiness, and with a mind full of faith, he lay there with his hands joined in salutation (añjali). Seeing the youth, the Blessed One reflected, 'This much merit is sufficient for this youth to be reborn in heaven,' and then departed. 

Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, without losing that rapture and happiness, passed away and was reborn in a twelve-yojana mansion in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. His father, after performing the funeral rites, went to the cemetery at dawn on the second day and wandered around weeping and lamenting, 'O my dear Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, how very painful it is!' The celestial son, looking at his own wealth and splendor, reflected, 'From where have I come here? What deed did I perform?' Realizing his previous existence, he saw the merit of the faith he had felt toward the Blessed One at the time of death and the simple act of joining his hands in salutation which draws the mind. He thought, 'How wonderful are the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones! How great is their power and majesty!' and with excessive faith and reverence for the Tathāgata, he wondered, 'What is the Brahmin Adinnapubbaka doing?' 

Seeing him weeping at the cemetery, he thought, 'This father of mine did not even provide me with medicine before, but now he weeps uselessly at the cemetery. I shall now cause him to feel spiritual urgency and establish him in merit.' Coming from the celestial realm in the form of Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, he stood near his father, raising his arms and crying out, 'O Moon! O Sun!' When the Brahmin saw him, he thought, 'This Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī has come,' and addressed him with a verse: 

'Adorned, wearing smooth earrings, wearing a garland, and smeared all over with red sandalwood, O youth, what sorrow has befallen you that you stand in the middle of the forest crying with your arms raised?' 

In that verse, 'alaṅkato' means having an adorned body. 'Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī' means having earrings made in a smooth form without showing the flower stalks or vines, so as not to irritate the body. Alternatively, 'Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī' means having pure earrings; it refers to earrings that have been heated, polished with genuine vermilion, washed, and then rubbed with pig's hair.
305:
The meaning is: 'Māladhārī' means one who carries flowers, one who has flowers to wear. 'Haricandanuassado' means one whose entire body is smeared all over with red sandalwood. The word 'Kiṃ' is a word of questioning. 'Dukkhito' means one who has reached suffering. Alternatively, taking 'Kiṃdukkhito' as a single term, it means 'By what suffering are you afflicted?'

Then the young deva said to the Brahmin:
"A golden, radiant chariot frame has arisen for me; but I cannot find a pair of wheels for it. Because of that grief, I shall give up my life."

Then the Brahmin said to the young deva:
"O good youth... tell me, shall I provide a pair of wheels made of gold, or made of gems, or made of rubies, or made of silver? I shall fulfill your need for a pair of wheels."

Hearing those words, the youth thought: "This Brahmin did not provide medical treatment for his son, yet seeing me who resembles his son, he weeps and says, 'I will make chariot wheels of gold and so on.' So be it... I shall rebuke him." Having thought thus, he asked, "How large a pair of wheels will you make for me?" When it was said, "I will make them as large as you desire," he requested, "I have need of the Moon and the Sun; give those Moon and Sun to me," and said:

That youth said to the Brahmin:
"Both the Moon and the Sun are seen here in the sky;
My golden chariot will be beautiful with that pair of wheels."

Then the Brahmin said to the young deva:
"Youth, you are indeed a fool, you who desire what should not be desired.
I think you will die, for you shall not obtain the Moon and the Sun."
306: Then the youth said to the Brahmin, "Is the one who weeps for the moon and sun, which are clearly visible, a fool, or is the one who weeps for the one who is not visible (the deceased) a fool?" and spoke thus: "The coming and going of both the moon and the sun are seen in their celestial paths; their radiance is evident. But the deceased who has passed away is no longer seen. Between the two of us weeping here, who is the more foolish?" Hearing these words, the Brahmin reflected, "This youth speaks what is fitting," and said: "Youth, you speak the truth; among those weeping, I alone am the more foolish. Like a child weeping for the moon, I have longed for the deceased who has passed away." Having said this, being freed from grief by the youth's words, and wishing to praise the youth, he recited these verses: "O youth, just as one might extinguish a fire fed with ghee by pouring water on it, you have extinguished all my distress, the fire of grief that was burning within me. You have truly pulled out the arrow of grief that rested in my heart, you who have removed the grief for my son from me who was overwhelmed by sorrow. O youth, having heard your words, I am one who has the arrow pulled out; I have become cool and tranquil. Now I no longer grieve, I no longer weep." 1208-10. In those verses, 'rathapañjaro' refers to the body of the chariot. 'Na vindāmi' means not obtaining. 'Bhaddamaṇava' is an address (vocative). 'Paṭipādayāmi' means I will provide or fulfill; the meaning is "do not give up your life because of the lack of a pair of wheels." 'Ubhayettha dissare' means both the moon and the sun are seen here in this sky. The letter 'ya' is a euphonic conjunction (sandhi), or the words should be split as 'ubhaye ettha'. 'Gamanāgamanaṃ' means the coming and going of the moon and sun are seen by way of their setting and rising day by day. There is also a Pali reading 'gamanogamanaṃ', meaning rising and setting are seen. 'Vaṇṇadhātu' refers to the pleasant, sparkling radiance (of the moon) due to its coolness, and the sharp, sparkling radiance (of the sun) due to its heat. 'Ubhayattha' should be understood as seeing the radiance in both the moon-mansion and the sun-mansion. 'Vīthiyā' means in the path of circulation, or in the paths in the sky such as Ajavīthi, Gajavīthi, Nāgavīthi, and so on. In the word 'ubhayettha', the conjunction 'ubhaye ettha' should be noted. 'Bālyataro' means one who is exceedingly foolish. Hearing these words, [the Brahmin thought], "Though I long for it, I long for what cannot be obtained..."
307:
"Entering" is the meaning. Vaṇṇadhātu refers to the radiant appearance that is pleasant and shimmering due to its cool nature, and the radiant appearance that is sharp and shimmering due to its hot nature. Ubhayattha means it should be applied as seeing the vaṇṇadhātu in both the moon and the sun. Vīthiyā refers to the sky, which is the path of travel, or paths such as the nāgavīthi. There is also a reading "ubhayettha", which is a word-combination of ubhaye ettha. Bālyataro means one who is exceedingly foolish.

Upon hearing these words, he stood reflecting on the benefits and harms: "Alas, I have been longing for what cannot be obtained and burning in vain with the fire of grief; what benefit is there for me in this fruitless ruin?" Then the deity discarded the appearance of the youth Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī and stood in his own divine form. The Brahmin, without looking at him [as a deity] but still addressing him as a youth, said: "Young man, you speak the truth," and so on. In that verse, "candaṃ viya dārako rudaṃ" means like a child crying, longing for the moon. "Kālakatābhipatthayiṃ" means I have longed for the one who has passed away. There is also a reading "abhipatthayaṃ".

1214-5. "Ādittaṃ" means burning with the fire of grief. "Nibbāpaye daraṃ" means he has quenched the distress and fever of grief. "Abbahī" means he has extracted it.

Then the Brahmin, having dispelled his grief and seeing the deity standing in divine form who had given him advice, asked "Who are you?":

"Are you a deva, a gandhabba, or Sakka Purindada? Who are you, or whose son? How may we know you?"

The deity said to the Brahmin:

"You yourself are weeping and lamenting for the son whom you cremated in the cemetery. That very person, having performed wholesome deeds, has reached the company of the Tidasa gods."
308:
(The deva) spoke about himself. In that verse, "how you weep and how you wail" refers to the weeping and shedding of tears for your son, Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī. Then the Brahmin said to the deva— "Whether little or much, we did not see you giving gifts in your own house. Nor did we see such observance of the Uposatha. By what meritorious deed did you reach the deva world?" (he asked). In that verse, the connection is: "Nor did we see such a deed of Uposatha."

Then the young man said to the Brahmin— "I was afflicted, suffering, and ill; I was in a state of pain in my own house. I saw the Buddha, the Sugata of perfect wisdom, who is free from the dust (of passions) and has crossed over doubt. With a joyful mind and a heart full of faith, I paid homage (añjali) to the Tathāgata. Having performed that meritorious deed, I have reached the company of the Tidasa (Thirty-three) gods."

1220-21. In that verse, 'ābādhika' means one who is possessed of an affliction. 'Dukkhita' means one who suffers because of that very affliction. 'Gilāna' means one who is becoming ill. 'Āturarūpa' means one whose body is greatly tormented by painful feelings. 'Vīgataraja' means one who is free from the dust of passion and so forth. 'Vītiṇṇakaṅkha' means one who has crossed over doubt because all doubts have been completely cut off. 'Anomapañña' means one who possesses perfect wisdom, meaning the Omniscient One (Sabbaññū). 'Akariṃ' means I did. 'Tāhaṃ' should be resolved as 'taṃ ahaṃ'. While the deva was speaking in this way, the Brahmin's entire body was filled with joy (pīti). Expressing that joy, the Brahmin said—
309:
“Wonderful indeed! Marvelous indeed! Such is the fruit of paying homage (añjalikamma). I too, with a joyful mind and a heart full of faith, go to the Buddha for refuge this very day,” he said. In that verse, it is called 'acchariya' (wonderful) because it is worthy of snapping one's fingers as it does not occur frequently; it is called 'abbhuta' (marvelous) because it has never happened before. By both terms, he showed only the quality of being amazing and said, “I too, with a joyful mind and a heart full of faith, go to the Buddha for refuge this very day.”

Then the deva, wishing to urge the Brahmin to take refuge and undertake the precepts, spoke these two verses— “With a heart full of faith, go to the Buddha for refuge this very day, and to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha. Likewise, undertake and practice the five precepts (sikkhāpada) which are unbroken and unspotted. Refrain quickly from taking life; avoid in this world what is not given; do not be a drinker of intoxicants, do not speak lies, and be content with your own wife.”

In those verses, “tatheva” (likewise) means— just as you, with a heart full of faith, went to the Buddha for refuge, saying, “The Blessed One is the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha),” likewise, with a heart full of faith, go to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha for refuge, saying, “The Dhamma is well-expounded, the Saṅgha has practiced well.” Alternatively— just as you, with a heart full of faith, went to the Triple Gem for refuge, likewise, with a heart full of faith, thinking, “These five precepts certainly bring welfare and happiness in this life and in the life to come,” undertake and practice the five precepts—which are the components of the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) or the means for the training in higher mind (adhicitta) and higher wisdom (adhipaññā)—without violation or defilement, so that they are unbroken and unspotted. This is the meaning. Thus urged by the deva to take refuge and undertake the precepts, the Brahmin, placing the deva's words on his head (accepting them with great respect)—
310:
"O deva, you desire my benefit, you desire my welfare. O deva, I will follow your words; you are my teacher," having spoken this verse and established himself in that instruction—

"I go to the Buddha for refuge, and also to the unsurpassed Dhamma (the nine supramundane states); I go to the Saṅgha of the Buddha (the God of Men) for refuge. I refrain quickly from taking life; I avoid in this world what is not given; I am not a drinker of intoxicants, nor do I speak lies; I shall be content with my own wife," he spoke these two verses. This statement is easily understood.

Thereafter, the deva thought, "I have done for the Brahmin what ought to be done; now he will go to the Blessed One of his own accord," and he vanished right there. The Brahmin, having developed great faith and reverence for the Blessed One and being urged by the deva, went towards the monastery, thinking, "I will approach the Monk Gotama." Seeing him go, the multitude followed him, thinking, "This Brahmin has not approached the Tathāgata for so long, but today he approaches because of grief for his son; what kind of Dhamma teaching will there be?"

The Brahmin approached the Blessed One, exchanged friendly greetings, and asked: "Venerable Gotama, is it possible to be reborn in heaven merely by faith in you, without giving any gift or keeping the precepts?" "Brahmin, did not the deva named Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī tell you the cause of his rebirth in the deva world this very morning at dawn?" the Blessed One said. At that moment, the deva Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī arrived with his celestial mansion (vimāna), and appearing in visible form, descended from the mansion, paid homage to the Blessed One, and stood at a respectful distance with his hands joined in salutation (añjali). Then the Blessed One, having recounted the good conduct performed by that deva to the assembly, and knowing the readiness of the assembly's mind, delivered the graduated teaching (sāmukkaṃsika-dhammadesanā). At the conclusion of the teaching, the deva, the Brahmin, and the assembled multitude—eighty-four thousand beings—attained the realization of the Dhamma (the Four Noble Truths).

## The Explanation of the Mansion of Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī (Maṭṭhakuṇḍalīvimānavaṇṇanā) is finished.
311:
## 10. Serīsakavimānavaṇṇanā

This verse-story beginning with "Suṇotha yakkhassa ca vāṇijānañca" is the Serīsakavimānavatthu. What is the origin of its occurrence? After the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, the Venerable Kumārakassapa arrived at the city of Setabyā together with five hundred monks. In that city, he dissuaded King Pāyāsi Rājañña, who had come to him, from his wrong views and established him in the right view. From that time on, the King became a seeker of merit, but because he was unaccustomed to the practice of giving to recluses and brahmins, he gave his donations without due respect (asakkaccaṃ). Consequently, when he passed away later on, he was reborn in the empty Serīsaka mansion in the realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā), which was devoid of attendants.

It is said that in the past, during the time of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha, an Arahant elder, after wandering for alms in a certain village, used to take his meal daily at a spot outside the village. Seeing that elder, a cowherd, with a heart full of faith, thinking, "The venerable one is weary from the heat of the sun," built a pavilion of branches using four Serīsa posts and offered it; it is also said that he planted a Serīsa tree near the pavilion. When he passed away, due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn among the devas of the Four Great Kings. As a sign of his previous deed, a Serīsa grove, beautiful at all times with flowers endowed with color and fragrance, appeared at the gate of his mansion. For that reason, the mansion came to be known as "Serīsaka." That deity, wandering through the realms of devas and humans during the interval between two Buddhas, was reborn as a human named Gavampati in the time of the present Buddha, being one of the four lay friends of the Elder Yasa, such as Vimala and others. Having heard the Dhamma of the Blessed One, he was established in the fruit of Arahantship. By the power of his former habit, that elder, seeing the empty mansion, would frequently go there for his day-abiding.

Later, seeing the deity Pāyāsi in that mansion, the elder asked, "Who are you, friend?" The deity replied, "Venerable sir, I am King Pāyāsi Rājañña, reborn here." The elder asked, "Were you not one of wrong views and distorted vision? How were you reborn here?" Then the deity Pāyāsi replied, "Venerable sir, I was dissuaded from wrong views by the Venerable Kumārakassapa. However, because I performed meritorious deeds without due respect, I was reborn in this empty mansion. It would be good, venerable sir, when you go to the world of men, to tell my followers..."
312:
"...'King Pāyāsi Rājañña, having given gifts without due respect, has been reborn in the empty Serīsaka mansion. You, however, should perform merits with due respect and set your hearts on being reborn in that place.' Out of compassion for him, the elder did as requested. Having heard the elder's words, those people also set their hearts accordingly, performed meritorious deeds, and were reborn in the Serīsaka mansion. King Vessavaṇa then appointed that Serīsaka deity as a road protector to rescue people traveling on the road in the Marubhūmi region, which is devoid of shade and water, from the dangers of non-human beings (amanussa).

Later, at another time, merchants residing in Aṅga and Magadha, having filled a thousand carts with merchandise, were traveling to the Sindhu-Sovīra region. Fearing the danger of the daytime heat in the Maru desert, they did not travel by day but traveled by night, using the stars as their guide. They lost their way and went in another direction. Among those merchants was a lay follower (upāsaka) who was faithful, devoted, endowed with virtue, and possessed the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for attaining Arahantship. He had joined the trade to support his parents. Desiring to favor that lay follower, the Serīsaka deity manifested himself along with his mansion. Having shown himself, he asked, "Why have you come to this sandy desert road, which is devoid of shade and water?" The merchants explained the circumstances of their arrival there. The verses of the dialogue between the deity and the merchants, illustrating that matter, exist. At the beginning, the elders who compiled the Dhamma (Dhamma-saṅgāhakas) placed two verses to show the connection of those verses:

'Listen to the meeting of the Yakkha and the merchants that took place then. Listen all of you to all that was well-spoken by one to the other.'

'There was a king named Pāyāsi, who has now gone to the company of the terrestrial devas (bhummā), and is famous. Rejoicing in his own mansion, that non-human addressed the humans.'

1228-9. In those verses, "Suṇotha" is a word of command to listen. It means, "Listen to what we are saying now." "Yakkhassa" means "of the deity (deva)." A deity is called "Yakkha" because he is worthy of worship by humans and some other deities. Alternatively, Sakka, the Four Great Kings, the followers of King Vessavaṇa, and even a man can be called "Yakkha." Such usage is found in places like, "This Yakkha (Sakka) lives very heedlessly; I shall strike terror into this Yakkha," and so on.
313:
Some deities are called "Yakkha" because they are worthy of worship. Alternatively, Sakka, the Four Great Kings, the attendants of King Vessavaṇa, and even a man can be called "Yakkha". This is true; in sentences such as "This Yakkha (Sakka) lives very heedlessly; what if I should cause this Yakkha to be dismayed?" (M. Ni. 1.393), Sakka is called "Yakkha". In sentences such as "Four Yakkhas with swords in hand," the Four Great Kings are referred to as Yakkhas. In sentences such as "Venerable Sir, there are powerful Yakkhas who have no faith in the Blessed One" (D. Ni. 3.276), the attendants of King Vessavaṇa are called Yakkhas. In sentences such as "To this extent is the purity of the Yakkha" (Su. Ni. 482), a man is called a Yakkha. In this context, however, it refers to the celestial son (Pāyāsi) who is an attendant of King Vessavaṇa. The phrase "Vāṇijāna ca" is spoken with the elision of the nasal (niggahīta) for the sake of poetic ease. "Samāgamo" means meeting. "Yattha" means in which sandy desert path. "Tadā" means at that time when they were traveling having lost their way. The phrase "Itaritarēna cāpī" means "and with each other"; this should be read in conjunction with the word "yathā". The meaning here is: Listen to the meeting of the celestial son Serīsaka and the merchants in that desert at that time. Also, listen with all your heart to the words they spoke well and discussed with each other. "Bhummānaṃ" refers to the Bhummadevas (earth-dwelling deities).

## Now these are the Yakkha's verses of inquiry:

In the crooked forest, a place of non-humans, in the waterless and foodless desert,
In the middle of the sandy path so difficult to traverse, O men whose minds are bewildered and lost, trembling with fear of dangers.

Here there are no fruits nor roots; there is no firewood and such, so how could there be food?
There is nothing else besides the dust and sand, which are burning, hot, and dreadful.

This region is extremely barren, like a heated iron pan, life-destroying, and similar to the other world;
This ancient abode of fierce ogres appears as if it has been cursed.
314:
Then, in what appearance and expecting what have you reached this place? Have you entered, having gathered in haste, out of greed, fear, or because you are utterly bewildered?

In that verse, 'Vaṅkē' refers to a place of doubt. It means a forest where those who enter feel doubt about their lives, thinking, 'Shall we live or shall we die?' 'Amanussaṭṭhāne' refers to a place frequented by non-humans such as Petas and ogres, or a place where humans should not go. 'Kantāre' refers to a waterless, difficult path. It is called 'kantāra' because one must carry water to cross it. Therefore, it says 'waterless'. Here, the word 'appa' denotes 'absence', as in 'appiccho' (few desires) or 'appanigghoso' (little noise). 'Vaṇṇupathassa majjhe' means in the middle of the sandy desert.

'Vaṅkaṃbhayā' means those who are terrified by dangers. For the sake of poetic ease, 'Vaṅkaṃbhayā' is used with an added nasal instead of 'Vaṅkabhayā'. This refers to the fear that arose in them even before entering the sandy desert. 'Naṭṭhamanā' means those whose minds are despondent, having lost mindfulness of the path, or those who have lost their way. 'Manussā' is an address to those people.

'Idhā' means in this sandy desert. 'Phalā' means that fruits such as mango, rose-apple, palm, and coconut do not exist. 'Mūlamayā ca' refers to creepers, roots, and the like. 'Upādānaṃ natthi' means that just as there is no food, there is not even firewood for making a fire. For what reason could there be food in this sandy desert? To show what is present there, it says 'Aññatra paṃsūhi' and so on.

'Ujjaṅgalaṃ' refers to a place that is even more extreme than a 'jaṅgala' (a harsh, dry, waterless region). Therefore, it says 'like a heated iron pan'. In the phrase 'Tattāmivaṃ kapālaṃ', the nasal is added for poetic ease, so it should be understood as 'Tattāmiva'. 'Anāyasaṃ' means that because there is no happiness (āya) here, it is called 'anāya', and because of that lack of happiness, life...
315:
...is destroyed; thus it is 'anāyasaṃ'. Alternatively, it is 'anāyasaṃ' because there is no iron (ayasa). 'Paralokena' means it is like hell (Niraya). Because hell is a world that is an enemy to beings, causing absolute harm, it is specifically called 'paraloka'. Hell is called 'āyasa' because it is made of iron on all sides; this desert is 'anāyasa' because it is not made of iron, yet it is shown to be like hell because it is a place where great suffering arises. Some read 'anassayaṃ', meaning a place that is not a support for happiness. 'Luddānamāvāsamidaṃ purāṇaṃ' means this place has been the abode of fierce ogres, ghosts, and the like since ancient times. 'Abhisattarūpo' means having an appearance as if cursed by ancient sages, saying, 'May it have such a harsh and terrifying form'; it means like one who has been cursed.

'Kena vaṇṇena' means for what reason? 'Kimāsamānā' means what are you longing for? 'Hi' is a mere particle. Some also read 'padesampi', meaning to such a place. 'Sahasā samecca' means entering in haste together without considering the disadvantages and advantages. 'Lobbhā bhayā' means either out of greed, or being enticed by someone who wishes them harm, or out of fear caused by being harassed by non-humans and the like. Alternatively, 'sampamūḷhā' means they entered this place because they had lost their way.

Now the merchants said:

"In the Magadha and Anga countries, we are caravan leaders who, having loaded many goods, travel to the land of Sindhu-Sovīra, desiring wealth and seeking profit.

Being unable to endure thirst during the day, and out of great compassion for our draft animals, we all come with this speed, traveling the path at night, which is the wrong time."
316:
“We, having taken a wrong path and gone astray, are wandering in the forest like blind men. In the midst of this desert path, which is extremely difficult to traverse, we are bewildered and do not know the directions. O Yakkha, having seen this noble mansion, which we have never seen before, and having seen you, we, longing for our lives beyond this, are delighted, joyful, and uplifted in mind.”

In that verse, ‘Magadhesu Angesu ca satthavāhā’ refers to those born and raised in the kingdoms of Magadha and Anga, residing there, who are caravan leaders and owners of caravans. ‘Paṇiyaṃ’ means trade goods or merchandise. ‘Te’ means ‘we’. ‘Yāmashe’ means ‘we go’. ‘Sindhusovīrabhūmiṃ’ refers to the regions of Sindhu and Sovīra. ‘Uddayaṃ’ refers to the benefit, advantage, and extra profit.

‘Anadhivāsayantā’ means being unable to endure (thirst). ‘Yoggānukampaṃ’ means showing compassion and care for the draft animals such as oxen. ‘Etena vegena’ means with such speed as we came before seeing you. ‘Rattiṃ maggaṃ paṭipannā’ means those who travel the path at night. ‘Vikāle’ means at an improper time.

‘Duppayātā’ means having traveled badly, having gone where there is no path, and thus having gone astray. ‘Andhākulā’ means bewildered like the blind; being like the blind due to the absence of the eye of wisdom capable of knowing the path, and thus being bewildered and lost because of confusion about the way. ‘Disaṃ’ refers to the direction to be taken, the direction where the Sindhu-Sovīra region is located. ‘Pamuḷhacittā’ means having a mind greatly confused by doubt regarding the directions.

‘Tavañca’ means ‘and you’. ‘Yakkha’ is a term of address. ‘Tatuttariṃ jīvitamāsamānā’ means that whereas doubt about life had arisen, thinking ‘There is no life for us beyond this,’ they are now longing for life beyond that. ‘Disvā’ means because of seeing. ‘Patītā’ means delighted. ‘Sumanā’ means having reached joy. ‘Udaggā’ means having an uplifted mind with lofty rapture.

When the merchants had thus made their circumstances clear, the deity asked with two verses: “O merchants, you who travel to the far shore of the ocean and to this path, the path to be traveled by reeds, the path to be traveled by driving in stakes, and to many other directions such as rivers and the rugged regions of mountains, in this manner for the sake of wealth... you who enter the kingdoms of others and travel while observing people living in various regions. You who have arrived and traveled thus, whether you have heard or seen...”
317:
When the merchants had thus made their circumstances clear, the deity asked again with two verses:

“O sirs, for the sake of wealth, you travel to the far shore of the ocean, to such a desert path, to the path traveled by holding onto reeds, to the path traveled by driving in stakes, to the difficult places of rivers and mountains, and to many directions.

You enter the kingdoms of other kings and travel while observing people living in various places. O sirs, as you travel thus, whatever wonder you have heard of or seen, we wish to hear of that wonder from you.”

The meaning of the verse: ‘Pāraṃ samuddassa’ means to the far shore of the ocean. ‘Imañca’ means such a nature. ‘Vaṇṇုံ’ means the sandy desert path (vaṇṇupatha). ‘Vettācaraṃ’ is the path to be traveled by binding and using reeds. ‘Saṅkupathaṃ’ is the path to be traveled by driving in stakes or stumps. ‘Nadiyo pana’ refers to rivers such as the Candabhāgā. ‘Pabbatānañca visamappadesā’ refers to the rugged regions of mountains. Thus, you go to many difficult directions for the sake of wealth. ‘Pakkhandiyāna’ means having entered the kingdoms of other kings. ‘Verajjake’ means people living in various foreign regions. O merchants, from you who have reached such a state, whatever wonder has been heard or seen, we wish to hear that wonder from you. He asks this, wishing them to speak of the wonderful nature of his own mansion.

Being thus questioned by the deity, the merchants replied:

“O Prince, we have never heard of nor seen anything more wonderful than this mansion of yours. Although we see all this, which surpasses the human form and is of perfect beauty, we are not satiated.
