In the sky, there are lakes with many fountains and white lotuses flowing. These trees of yours are always endowed with fruit, and from those trees, exceedingly fragrant scents waft abroad.”
318:
“There are pillars of beryl a hundred cubits high, and long-faceted pillars made of crystal and coral. There are also pillars made of masāragalla stone and red rubies. These pillars are made of the radiant Jotirasa stone.

Above those pillars stands this mansion of yours with a thousand pillars and incomparable power; it is truly magnificent. It is interspersed with jewels, mixed with golden railings, and well-covered with plates of fine gold.

This mansion has the color of molten Jambonada gold, is very smooth and beautiful, and is endowed with palace stairways. It is firm, stable, beautiful in form, and its parts are well-joined. It is exceedingly worth looking at and delightful.

Amidst the jewels, many kinds of food and drink are obtained. Surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs, you, O deity, are honored with praise and salutation, amidst the sounding of musical instruments such as the muraja and ālambara drums.

Just as King Vessavaṇa delights in the lake named Nalinī, you, O deity, who are endowed with all virtues and are beyond thought, delight in this noble and heart-pleasing palace mansion, awakening the host of celestial nymphs.

Are you a god, or a Yakkha, or are you Sakka, the king of gods, in human form? The merchants, the leaders of the caravan, ask you. O deity, please tell us what your name is.”
319:
1240-2. In those verses, the word "Kumāra" (youth) is used to address the deity because he remains in the first stage of life. The word "Sabba" (all) is spoken in reference to the deity and the pleasures associated with his mansion (vimāna). "Pokkharañño" refers to lotus ponds. "Satamussitāse" means one hundred cubits high. "Silāpavāḷassa" means made of crystal and coral. "Āyataṃsā" means having long edges, or it means being long and having eight, sixteen, thirty-two, or more facets.

"Tesūpari" means above those pillars. "Sādhumidaṃ" means "this mansion of yours is very excellent." "Ratanantaraṃ" means endowed with various other gems in the walls, pillars, stairs, and so forth. "Kañcanavedimissaṃ" means accompanied by or surrounded by a golden railing (vedikā). "Tapanīyapaṭṭehi ca sādhuchannaṃ" means well-covered in various places with roofs made of gold and many kinds of gems.

"Jambonaduttattamidaṃ" means "this mansion of yours has a brilliance mostly like molten Jambonada gold." "Sumaṭṭho pāsādasopānaphalūpapanno" means that every part of that mansion is very smooth and polished, and it is endowed with various intervening palaces, special stairways, and delightful planks. "Daḷho" means firm and stable. "Vaggū" means beautiful in form and well-lofty. "Susaṅgato" means the parts are well-joined, having palace components that are mutually proportionate. "Atīva nijjhanakhamo" means very worthy of being looked at because of its radiant nature. "Manuñño" means delightful.

"Ratanantarasmiṃ" means inside the mansion which is made of gems, or is excellent like a gem. "Bahuannapānaṃ" means there is an abundance of pleasant food and drink available. "Muraja-ālambara-tūriya-ghuṭṭho" means constantly resounded with the sounds of drums, Ālambara drums, and other musical instruments. "Abhivanditosi" means you are worshipped or praised. Therefore, it says "for praise and reverence" (thutivandanāya).

"Acintiyo" means having inconceivable power. "Naḷinyā" means in the pleasure ground of this name, just as the Great King Vessavaṇa rejoices, so do you rejoice—this is the connection.
320:
"Āsīti" means "are you?" or "do you become?". "Devindo" is Sakka, the king of gods. "Manussabhūto" means born among humans, a true human being. The word "Yakkho" is used because, even after asking if he is a god, they still suspect him of being a yakkha (spirit).

Now, the deity, wishing to make himself known, said:
"I am the yakkha named Serīsaka; I am the guardian of the wilderness on the sandy desert path. I protect this region, acting according to the word of King Vessavaṇa."

In that verse, "Ahamhi yakkho" means "I am a yakkha." "Kantāriyo" means one appointed to the wilderness for the purpose of protection. "Gutto" means a guardian. Therefore, he says "Abhipālayāmi" (I protect).

Now the merchants, wishing to ask about his kamma and so on, said:
"Did you obtain this delightful thing by chance without a cause, or did it arise as a result of evolution, or did you do it yourself, or was it given by the gods? The merchants, the caravan leaders, ask you: how did you obtain this delightful thing?"

In that verse, "Adhiccaladdhaṃ" means obtained by chance, occurring coincidentally without regarding a cause. "Pariṇāmajaṃ te" means transformed through the nature of necessity and coincidence, or transformed by time. "Sayaṃkataṃ" means done by yourself, or brought into existence by yourself through divine power. "Udāhu devehi dinnaṃ" means bestowed out of favor by the gods whom you have pleased.

Now the deity, rejecting all four of those ways and pointing only to merit (puñña), spoke the verse:
"This delightful mansion of mine was not obtained by chance, nor is it the result of evolution, nor was it made by myself, nor was it given by the gods. It is through my own non-depraved meritorious deeds that I have obtained this delightful mansion."
321:
Hearing those words, the merchants once again asked about the nature of merit, attributing those four ways to merit itself with the verse beginning "Nādhiccaladdhaṃ": "What was your vow? What was your holy life? Of what well-practiced conduct is this the result? The merchants, the caravan leaders, ask you: how did you obtain this mansion?" In that verse, "Vata" means a self-imposed observance or vow. "Brahmacariya" means the noble or holy life.

Again, the deity, setting aside those reasons and wishing to show the merit he himself had accumulated, said: "When I ruled as king over the Kosalans, I was known as Pāyāsi. At that time, I held the nihilistic view (natthika-diṭṭhi), was miserly, of evil conduct, and was an annihilationist (ucchedavādī). There was a monk named Kumārakassapa, who was very learned, an eloquent speaker, and endowed with noble qualities. At that time, he preached the Dhamma to me and removed the thorns of my wrong views. Having heard his Dhamma talk, I declared myself a lay follower (upāsaka). I became one who abstained from taking life, I avoided taking what was not given in the world, I did not drink intoxicants, nor did I speak falsehood, and I was content only with my own wife."
322:
“That practice was my undertaking; that indeed was the holy life (brahmacariya). This is the result of that well-practiced conduct. Only through those pure and non-evil meritorious deeds have I obtained this mansion (vimāna),” he said. That statement is easily understood.

Then the merchants, seeing the deity (devaputta) and his mansion with their own eyes and believing in the fruit of kamma, wishing to make known their faith in the fruit of their own kamma, spoke these two verses:

“Wise men indeed speak the truth; the words of the wise are not otherwise. Wherever a person of meritorious deeds goes, there they rejoice, obtaining the desired sensual pleasures as they wish.

Wherever there is sorrow, lamentation, killing, binding, and affliction, there the person of evil deeds goes; they are never released from a miserable state (duggati),” they said.

In those verses, ‘sokapariddavo’ means sorrow and lamentation. ‘Parikkileso’ means the aforementioned dangers that are the cause of suffering.

While the merchants were speaking thus, a ripe fruit pod, having matured and loosened from its stalk, fell from a Sirīsa tree at the gate of the mansion. Because of that falling fruit, the deity, along with his retinue, became dejected (domanassa). Seeing that state, the merchants spoke this verse:

“O young deity, at this moment, the people seem utterly bewildered; they are as if withered, like those stuck in mud. What is the cause of this unhappiness (appaccayo) for this retinue and for you?”

In that verse, ‘sammūḷharūpova’ means being as if in a state of complete bewilderment through the power of sorrow. ‘Jano’ means the assembly of deities. ‘Asmiṃ muhutte’ means at this...”
323:
...moment. ‘Kalalīkato’ means made like mud; the meaning is turbid like water mixed with mud. ‘For this retinue and for you’ refers to your attendants and yourself. ‘Appaccayo’ means unhappiness (domanassa).

Hearing those words, the deity said:
‘O friends, these divine and fragrant scents from the Sirīsa grove waft all around.
Dispelling the darkness day and night, they make this mansion fragrant from every side.
Each fruit pod of these Sirīsa trees falls after the passing of a hundred years. Since the time I was reborn here in this body, a hundred human years have passed.
O friends, having stayed in this mansion for five hundred years, I shall pass away due to the exhaustion of life and the exhaustion of merit (puñña). I am bewildered by that very sorrow,’ he said.

In that verse, ‘sirīsavanā’ means from the Sirīsa grove. By the word ‘tātā’, he addresses the merchants. These divine scents, which are evident to both you and me, are extremely fragrant and waft all around. When these divine scents waft in this way, they not only make this mansion well-perfumed but also dispel the darkness with their own radiance. Therefore, it is said, ‘dispelling the darkness day and night.’

1260-61. ‘Imesaṃ’ means of the Sirīsa trees. ‘Sipāṭikā’ means the fruit pod. ‘Phallati’ means ripening and loosening from the stalk, or reaching the stage where the pod bursts and only the stalk remains. ‘A hundred human years have passed’ means that since the fruit pod of this Sirīsa tree falls only after a hundred years have passed, and it has now fallen, a hundred years by human reckoning have passed for me. ‘Yadagge’ means from the time when. ‘Kāyamhi idha’ means in this divine assembly...”
324:
...he was reborn. For me, the lifespan is five hundred years by the reckoning of the deities; therefore, he shows that he is greatly bewildered by the power of sorrow, thinking, “My life is coming to an end.” Thus he said, “Having seen five hundred years... I am bewildered by that very sorrow.”

Then the merchants, wishing to console him, said:
“How could such a one as you grieve, having obtained an incomparable mansion for so long? Those who are reborn for only a short time, those of little merit, they are the ones who should surely grieve.”

In that verse, the meaning is: while those with short lives and little merit might grieve on account of death, how could one such as you, endowed with such divine power and a lifespan of nine million years, grieve? You should not grieve at all.

Being consoled by just those words, the deity, accepting their speech and wishing to give them guidance, spoke this verse:
“The affectionate words you speak to me are appropriate and are words of advice for me. O friends, you are protected by me; go safely with that protection to wherever you wish.”

In that verse, ‘anucchaviṃ’ means appropriate; that is a fitting thing for you to say. ‘Ovadiyañca metaṃ’ means this is something that should be said to me by you by way of advice. Because (yaṃ) you speak affectionate words (peyyavācaṃ) to me, such as “How could you grieve?”, etc. Or the construction is: that speaking with affectionate words is appropriate for you. Alternatively, because (yaṃ) you speak affectionate words, I have done what is appropriate and what should be done according to the advice given to me. What is that? He said, “O friends,” and so on. In that text, ‘mayānuguttā’ means: in this desert possessed by non-humans (amanussa), I have protected you until the crossing of the desert; go safely (sotthiṃ) and at ease as you please. 

Then the merchants, wishing to manifest their gratitude...”
325:
“Desiring wealth and longing for profit, we shall go to the land of Sindhusoวีra and, according to our current undertaking, with full generosity, we shall perform a grand festival of worship for the deity Serīsaka.” Thus they spoke the verse.

In that verse, ‘yathāpayogā’ means having effort consistent with the promise made now. ‘Paripuṇṇacāgā’ means having complete generosity, having the sacrifice of one's ability for the sake of a vast and noble worship. ‘Mahaṃ’ means a grand festival of worship.

Then, the deity, wishing to reject the worship by festival and desiring to urge the merchants toward the duties that should be performed, spoke this verse:

“Do not perform the worship for Serīsaka,
And all the benefits you speak of shall come to pass.
Avoid evil unwholesome deeds,
And establish yourselves in the practice of Dhamma.”

In that verse, ‘yaṃ vadetha’ refers to the words spoken such as “We shall go...” while longing for a safe arrival at the region of Sindhusoวีra and for great profit and gain there. All that shall happen for you just as desired; have no doubt in that matter. As for you, from this time forth, avoid and shun evil unwholesome deeds such as taking life. ‘Dhammānuyogaṃ’ means the repeated practice of wholesome qualities such as giving (dāna). ‘Adhiṭṭhahātha’ means to practice repeatedly; it shows that this very practice is the worship of the deity Serīsaka.

Desiring to favor a certain lay follower (upāsaka) and wishing to provide protection and warding for those merchants, the deity spoke these verses, praising and pointing out the virtues of that lay follower:

“In this assembly of people, there is a lay follower,
Learned, endowed with virtue,
Faithful, generous, and very kind,
Discerning, contented, and wise.”
326:
“Knowing, he would not speak a lie; he would not intend to oppress or harm others. He would not engage in slander that causes division between two people; he would speak only gentle and polite words.

Respectful, humble, with a disciplined body, free from evil conduct, and pure in higher virtue (adhisīla), that person also supports his mother and father righteously; he has a pure livelihood.

I think that lay follower seeks wealth only for the sake of his mother and father, not for his own sake. With a mind inclined toward Nibbāna, he will practice the holy life (brahmacariya) when his mother and father have passed away.

Upright, not crooked, not deceitful, not fraudulent, that person would not speak even with a permissible hint (of deception). Being such a one, a doer of good deeds, established in Dhamma, how could he encounter suffering?

Because of that lay follower, I have manifested myself to you; therefore, O merchants, see to it that you practice the Dhamma. If you were to travel in this forest without that lay follower, you would quickly turn to ashes, being confused and ruined like the blind due to dangers. Association with such a virtuous person is indeed pleasant.”

In that verse, ‘saṅghe’ means the assembly of beings. ‘Vicakkhaṇo’ means one who is skilled in various duties to be performed. ‘Santusito’ means one who is easily contented. ‘Mutīmā’ is called ‘mutimā’ because he knows the benefits of this world and the next through knowledge such as the ownership of one's kamma (kammassakata-ñāṇa).

‘Sañjānamāno na musā bhaṇeyya’ means he would not speak a deliberate lie while knowing. ‘Vebhūtikaṃ’ refers to slanderous speech called ‘vebhūtika’ because it causes division between two people who are in harmony; he would not do or speak such things.
327:
‘Sappaṭisso’ refers to one who possesses gentleness (soracca) along with respect, because of having a humble manner toward those worthy of respect. ‘Adhisīle’ refers to the training in higher virtue that should be observed by a lay follower. ‘Ariyavuttī’ means pure livelihood.

‘Nekkhammapoṇo’ means one who is inclined toward Nibbāna. ‘Cariဿati brahmacariyaṃ’ means he will practice the noble practice of monkhood in the Dispensation (Sāsana).

‘Lesakappena’ means by way of a permissible hint. ‘Na ca vohareyya’ means he would not utter words by way of fraud or deceit. ‘Dhamme ṭhito kinti labhetha dukkhaṃ’ means, in the manner described, how or in what way could one who is established in Dhamma, a practitioner of Dhamma, and a practitioner of fairness, reach suffering?

‘Taṃkāraṇā’ means because of that reason, for the sake of that lay follower. ‘Pātukatomhi attanā’ means I have manifested myself to you personally. There is also a reading ‘attānaṃ’, meaning “I have made myself manifest to you.” ‘Tasmā’ means because I, respecting the Dhamma and protecting that Dhamma, also protect you; therefore, look at the Dhamma, look upon it by considering that only the Dhamma should be practiced. ‘Aññatra teniha bhasmī bhavetha’ means if you had come to this sandy desert without that lay follower, you would have turned to ashes, being without refuge and without protection. ‘Khippamānena’ means by such casting away, blaming, or oppressing. ‘Lahuṃ’ means very easy. ‘Parena’ means excessively or by other forms of oppression. Therefore, association with a virtuous person is indeed pleasant. The meaning is that because that lay follower is established in patience and gentleness, even if spoken to by someone, he does not strike back (retaliate).

The merchants, wishing to know specifically about the lay follower who was thus praised in general, spoke this verse:

“O deity, for whose sake you have come here out of compassion, what is his name? What work does he do? What is his name and what is his clan? We also wish to see him. Gains indeed come to him whom you cherish.”

In that verse, ‘kiṃ nāmo so’ is an inquiry into what that being is called by name. ‘Kiñca karoti kammaṃ’ is an inquiry into what kind of work he does, such as farming or trading.
328:
"What is his name?" refers to the name given by parents, such as Tissa or Phussa; it asks what his name is, or what his clan (gotta) is, such as Bhaggava or Bhāradvāja. "The one whom you cherish" means the one you love and hold dear.

Now, the deity (devaputta), wishing to describe that lay follower (upāsaka) by way of name, clan, and so forth, said:

"That lay follower is a barber named Sambhava,
who lives by the art of grooming (kocchaphala).
Know him as your servant;
do not mistreat him, for he is one who dearly loves virtue."

In that verse, 'kappako' means a barber. 'Sambhava-nāmadheyyo' means one whose name is Sambhava. 'Kocchaphala-ūpajīvī' means one who lives depending on the comb (koccha) and the result (phala). Therein, 'koccha' refers to the barber's art of scraping and shaving the hair to make it neat. 'Pesiyo' means an attendant or one who performs services as commanded.

Now, the merchants, having recognized that lay follower, said:

"O deity, we know the person you speak of, but we did not know he was endowed with such qualities.
O deity, having heard your noble words, we too shall honor him."

In that verse, 'jānāmase' means "we know that person personally as you describe." 'Ediso' means "we did not know him to be such a person endowed with qualities as praised by you, the deity"; the meaning is that they were like those who were ignorant.

Now, the deity, wishing to take those merchants up to his mansion (vimāna) and give them an exhortation, said:

"Whatever people are in this caravan, whether young, old, or middle-aged,
let them all ascend to the mansion; let the stingy see the fruit of merit."
329:
The deva spoke the verse beginning with "Ye keci imasmiṃ satthe manussā" to bring the merchants into his mansion and to instruct them. "O merchants, in this caravan, there are all sorts of people—young, old, or middle-aged. Let all those people ascend to this mansion. Let those with miserly hearts see the fruits of meritorious deeds," he said. In that verse, "mahantā" refers to the elderly. "Ālambantu" means let them ascend. "Kadariyā" refers to those who are stingy and not in the habit of giving.

## Now at the conclusion, six verses were spoken by the Dhamma-reciters:

"All those merchants, saying 'I first, I first,' and placing that barber lay follower at their head, all ascended the mansion of the Serīsaka deva, which was like Masakkasāra, the city of Sakka.

All those merchants, saying 'I first, I first,' declared their status as lay followers. They abstained from taking life and avoided taking what was not given in the world. They did not drink intoxicants, nor did they speak lies, and they were content with their own wives.

All those merchants, saying 'I first, I first,' having declared their status as lay followers, the caravan departed, rejoicing again and again, permitted by the psychic power of the yakkha (deva).

Having gone to the land of Sindhu-Sovīra, those who desired wealth and sought profit, being endowed with appropriate effort, were filled with gains and benefits, and returned safely to the city of Pāṭaliputta.

Having reached their homes in safety and being reunited with their wives and children, being joyful, glad, happy, and satisfied, they performed a grand festival for the Serīsaka deva. They also constructed a precinct named Serīsaka, complete with walls, gates, and towers."

Such is the nature of associating with the virtuous. Relying on the grace of the Dhamma brings great benefit. Through the favor shown for the sake of a single lay follower, all beings attained happiness. In that verse, "ahaṃ pure" means the competitive effort expressed as "I first, I first." The repetition of "te tattha sabbeva" and "sabbeva te" is intended to show that all the merchants ascended the mansion with great enthusiasm, without anyone facing any danger.
330:
Associating with the virtuous is of such a nature; attending to the virtues of the Dhamma brings great benefit. For the sake of a single lay follower, through the assistance provided, all beings have indeed attained happiness.

In that verse, 'ahaṃ pure' means the act of doing something with the pride of 'I first, I first.' The reason for saying 'sabbeva te' again after saying 'te tattha sabbeva' is to show that just as all those merchants made an effort to ascend the mansion, in that same way, all were able to ascend it, and no one faced any danger while ascending. In the phrase 'masakkasāraṃ viya vāsavassa,' 'Masakkasāra' refers to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, or it can refer to all celestial realms. Here, however, it should be understood as the mansion of Sakka. Therefore, it is said, 'like the Masakkasāra mansion of Sakka.'

1277-8. Then those merchants, seeing the mansion and having settled faith, stayed within the deity's exhortation and established themselves in the Refuges and the Precepts; through the power of that deity, they reached their desired destination in safety. Therefore, the verses beginning with 'te tattha sabbeva' were spoken. In that verse, the construction (yojanā) is that the caravan departed, rejoicing again and again through the power of the deity. If it is asked who gave permission or caused them to rejoice, it is clearly the deity.

'Yathāpayogā' means having put forth effort according to their own inclinations. 'Paripuṇṇalābhā' means having abundant gains. 'Akkhataṃ' means reaching the city of Pāṭaliputta without danger, or it means reaching without illness, without oppression, and without obstacles.

'Saṅgharaṃ' means one's own home. 'Sotthivanto' means being endowed with safety and well-being. By the four words beginning with 'ānandī,' only the state of being joyful is meant. 'Serīsakaṃ te pariveṇaṃ māpayiṃsu' means that those merchants, out of gratitude and to fulfill their promised word, built and offered a residential precinct (pariveṇa) named 'Serīsaka' after the deity's name, which was worthy of being looked at in its proportions, and was complete with palaces, pinnacled houses (kūṭāgāra), night quarters, and so on, surrounded by walls and equipped with gate-towers.
331:
"Etādisā" means of such a nature, having the meaning of preventing harm and accomplishing benefit in this way. "Mahatthikā" means having great benefit and advantage. "Dhammaguṇānaṃ" refers to the virtues of the Dhamma which are unerring. For the benefit of a single being (the lay follower), all beings included in the caravan have reached happiness and safety.

The lay follower named Sambhava, having heard the composition of verses that arose through the conversation between the deva Pāyāsi and those merchants, memorized them as he heard them and reported them to the elders. Some teachers, however, say that the deva Pāyāsi told the Venerable Sambhava Thera. The great elders, headed by the Venerable Yasa Thera, included that account in the Second Council. The lay follower Sambhava, after the passing of his parents, went forth as a monk and was established in Arahantship.

## The Explanation of the Serīsaka Mansion is finished.

## 11. Sunikkhitta-vimāna-vaṇṇanā

"Uccamidaṃ maṇithūṇaṃ vimānaṃ" and so forth—this is the story of the Sunikkhitta Mansion. What is the origin of this story? It happened while the Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī. At that time, the Venerable Mahā-Moggallāna, while wandering on a celestial journey as mentioned above, arrived at the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. At that moment, a certain deva, standing at the door of his mansion, saw the Venerable Mahā-Moggallāna and, with a heart full of respect and reverence, approached him, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, and stood with palms joined in salutation.

It is said that in the past, after the Parinibbāna of the Kassapa Buddha, when his relics were enshrined and a golden stupa one yojana in height was built, the fourfold assembly would approach from time to time and make offerings to the stupa with perfumes, flowers, incense, and so on. At that stupa, after other people had finished their flower offerings and left, a certain lay follower saw the flowers that were poorly placed at the site of offering. Rearranging those very flowers properly there, he made a flower offering that was beautiful, pleasing, and specially arranged in an orderly manner. Having done so, taking that as an object of meditation and repeatedly recollecting the virtues of the Teacher with a confident mind, he kept that merit in his heart.
332:
Later, after he passed away, by the power of that meritorious deed, he was reborn in a golden mansion twelve yojanas in size in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, possessing great power and a large retinue. With reference to that, it is said: "At that moment, a certain deva... stood." Then, the Venerable Mahā-Moggallāna, beginning by praising the prosperity the deva had attained, asked about the good deeds he had performed in the past with these verses:

"This mansion of yours, with its jeweled pillars, is very high; it is twelve yojanas all around. Seven hundred magnificent pinnacled buildings, with columns of lapis lazuli and covered with beautiful rugs, are splendid.

There you stay, drink, and eat; and divine lutes sound melodiously. Here in this mansion are the fivefold divine sensual pleasures, and goddesses clad in golden ornaments dance.

Due to what deed is your complexion such as this? Due to what deed is your prosperity fulfilled here? And all the enjoyments that are dear to your heart, do they arise for you?

O deva of great power, I ask you: what merit did you perform when you were a human being? Due to what deed do you have such shining power, and why does your complexion illuminate all directions?"

That deva also told the deed he had performed to the Venerable Mahā-Moggallāna with these verses. To show this, the Recorders of the Council said:

"That deva, being delighted and questioned by Moggallāna, explained the problem when asked, showing of which deed this was the fruit:

'By well-arranging and establishing the poorly placed flowers at the stupa of the Sugata, I possess great psychic power and great majesty, and I am endowed with divine sensual pleasures.'"
333:
"'Due to that merit, I have such a complexion; due to that merit, my desire is fulfilled here. All the enjoyments that are dear to my heart also arise for me.

O monk of great power, I shall tell you the merit I performed when I was a human being. Due to that merit, I have such shining power, and my complexion illuminates all directions,' (the deva said).

In that verse, 'dunnikkhittaṃ mālaṃ' refers to flowers that were not well-placed because they were not arranged in an orderly manner at the place of offering at the stupa, or flowers that were poorly placed because they were blown down by the wind. 'Sunikkhipitvā' means having placed them well, making them beautiful and pleasing through special arrangement. 'Patiṭṭhapetvā' means establishing the flowers through special classification and so forth. Or, it should be understood here that while offering those flowers, one establishes meritorious states in one's own continuity of mind, intending them for the stupa of the Teacher. The rest is just as previously explained.

When the deva thus revealed his own good deeds, the Elder, having preached the Dhamma to that deva, returned and reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, making that the starting point of the discourse, preached the Dhamma to the assembled great crowd. That teaching was beneficial to the great crowd.

## The Explanation of the Sunikkhitta Mansion is finished.

## Concluding Remarks

This teaching of the Vimānavatthu, which is of such extent, which brings welfare to all the world, which reveals the prosperity of the divine mansions of the deities and the causes thereof, and which makes clear that even small acts of merit yield grand fruits due to the perfection of the field of the mind—this was chanted in the Khuddaka Nikāya under the name "Vimānavatthu" by the Great Sages who were skilled in the matters of discourse and who thoroughly understood the subject matter.

To clarify the meaning of that Vimānavatthu, relying on the methods of the ancient teachers, this commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) has been undertaken by me.

Because it reveals the ultimate meanings therein as is appropriate, it is known by the name "Paramatthadīpanī." This commentary, with its clear-cut decisions, has reached its complete conclusion in Pāḷi, measuring seventeen bhāṇavāras in length.

By the power of the merit I have acquired through the composition of this commentary, may all beings, having entered the Dispensation of the Lord of the World through pure conduct such as virtue (sīla) and so forth, become partakers of the taste of liberation (vimuttirasa).

May the Dispensation of the Fully Enlightened One endure long in the world. May all living beings always be respectful towards that Dispensation.
335:
May the rain-god also send down rain properly in due season. May the lord of the earth, delighting in the True Dhamma, rule the world only with righteousness.

## Thus, the explanation of the meaning of the Vimānavatthu,
## in the Commentary of the Khuddaka Nikāya named Paramatthadīpanī,
## composed by the Great Teacher Dhammapāla, a resident of the Badaratittha Monastery, is finished.
